chapters.n: The book of Job opens like a story: a man in a land called Uz who is blameless and devoted to God. The book will wrestle with a hard question — why do good people suffer? The Lord later reminded Joseph Smith in Liberty Jail of Job’s trials.

f.g: A region probably east or southeast of Israel, toward Edom or northern Arabia (Lamentations 4:21).
Hebrew tam — whole, blameless, of complete integrity; not “never made a mistake.”
Avoided, turned away from.

chapters.n: Job has seven sons and three daughters. Seven and three were numbers of completeness — his family is perfectly blessed.
He is enormously wealthy in livestock and servants — the richest man in the East. Wealth in that culture was measured in animals.

f.g: Pairs of oxen used for plowing.
Female donkeys, valued for milk and breeding.
The peoples east of Israel, known for their wisdom (1 Kings 4:30).

chapters.n: His grown children take turns hosting feasts, and the brothers include their sisters. It is a picture of a happy, close family.

f.g: Each on his own day, perhaps birthdays.

chapters.n: After each round of feasts, Job rises early to offer sacrifices for each child, just in case they had sinned in their hearts. He acts as the family’s priest, as patriarchs did before the law of Moses.

f.g: Had them ritually purified.
The Hebrew says “blessed God,” a polite substitute scribes used to avoid writing “curse God.”

chapters.n: The scene shifts to heaven, where the “sons of God” — heavenly beings — present themselves before the Lord. Among them comes “the Satan,” meaning “the adversary” or accuser.

f.g: Hebrew ha-satan, “the adversary” or “the accuser.”

chapters.n: The Lord asks where he has been. Satan answers that he has been roaming the earth — restless, watching, looking for faults.

f.w: going to and fro in the earth

chapters.n: The Lord points out Job with obvious pride: there is no one like him on earth. The Lord calls him “my servant,” a title of honor.

f.g: Literally “Have you set your heart on” — have you noticed.

chapters.n: Satan’s challenge is the question of the whole book: does Job serve God for nothing? In other words, is his goodness real, or is it just a good deal?

f.g: For nothing — without reward or self-interest.

chapters.n: Satan argues that God has put a protective hedge around Job and blessed everything he does. Of course Job is faithful — it pays.

f.g: A protective fence — divine protection.

chapters.n: Take it all away, Satan says, and Job will curse you to your face. He claims that no one loves God freely.

f.g: Strike his possessions.

chapters.n: The Lord allows Satan to test Job’s possessions but not to harm Job himself. Satan has power only within limits God sets.

f.w: only upon himself put not forth thine hand

chapters.n: Back on earth, on a festive day while Job’s children are feasting at the oldest brother’s house, disaster begins.
A messenger arrives with news about Job’s plowing oxen and the donkeys grazing nearby.
Raiders from Sheba steal the animals and kill the servants. Only one survives to bring the news.

f.g: Raiders from Sheba, in southern Arabia.

f.w: I only am escaped alone to tell thee
f.g: This refrain repeats four times, like hammer blows.

chapters.n: Before he finishes, a second messenger reports that “the fire of God” — likely lightning — has burned up the sheep and the shepherds.

f.g: Probably lightning; compare 1 Kings 18:38.

chapters.n: A third messenger arrives: Chaldean raiders in three groups have stolen the camels and killed the servants.

f.g: Raiders from Mesopotamia; long before they became the Babylonian empire.
Three raiding parties.

chapters.n: Then the fourth messenger comes with the worst news of all, about Job’s children at their brother’s house.
A violent wind from the desert struck the house, and it collapsed on them; all his children are dead. In one day Job loses everything, from his wealth to his beloved family.

f.w: a great wind from the wilderness
f.g: Probably a desert whirlwind striking all four corners.
Hebrew can mean “young people,” including his daughters.

chapters.n: Job tears his robe and shaves his head — signs of grief — and falls to the ground. But in his grief, he worships.

f.g: Tore his outer robe in mourning.

chapters.n: Job’s famous words: I was born with nothing, and I will leave with nothing. The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away — blessed be His name. His faith is real.

f.w: Naked came I out of my mother's womb

f.g: There — to the earth, the “mother” of all.

f.w: blessed be the name of the LORD

chapters.n: Through all this, Job did not sin or accuse God of wrongdoing. Satan’s prediction has failed.

f.g: Blamed God for wrongdoing.

f.w: In all this Job sinned not

chapters.n: A second heavenly council scene, deliberately echoing the first. The repetition signals that a second, harder test is coming.
The Lord asks the same question and receives the same answer. Satan is still roaming, still looking for weakness.

f.w: From going to and fro in the earth

chapters.n: The Lord points to Job again: he still holds on to his integrity, even though Satan urged God to ruin him for no reason. Job’s suffering was not a punishment for sin.

f.g: Keeps his wholeness and faithfulness intact.
For no reason — the same Hebrew word as “for nought” in Job 1:9.

chapters.n: Satan replies with a proverb: “Skin for skin” — a person will give up anything to save his own life. Losing possessions and even children wasn’t enough, he claims.

f.g: Probably a trading proverb: a man will trade anything for his own skin.

chapters.n: Strike his body, Satan says, and he will curse you. His accusation is that human faith is ultimately selfish.
The Lord allows it, but sets a firm limit: Job’s life must be spared.
Satan strikes Job with painful sores covering his whole body, from the soles of his feet to the top of his head.

f.g: Painful, inflamed skin sores; the exact disease is unknown.
Top of the head.

chapters.n: Job sits in the ash heap outside town, scraping his sores with a piece of broken pottery. The richest man in the East now sits in the garbage dump.

f.g: A broken piece of pottery.
Likely the town’s ash and rubbish heap, where outcasts sat.

chapters.n: Job’s wife, who has also lost all her children and wealth, speaks in despair: Why hold on? Curse God and die. Her words echo exactly what Satan predicted.

f.w: Dost thou still retain thine integrity?

f.g: Again the Hebrew politely says “bless,” meaning “curse.”

chapters.n: Job gently rebukes her for speaking like a godless person, then asks: should we accept only good from God and never trouble? He still does not sin with his words.

f.g: Hebrew nabal — morally foolish, godless, not merely unintelligent.

f.w: shall we receive good at the hand of God, and shall we not receive evil?

f.g: Here meaning trouble or misfortune, not sin.

chapters.n: Three friends from different lands arrange to come comfort him. Their names and homelands suggest wise men from the regions east of Israel.

f.g: From Teman in Edom, known for its wisdom (Jeremiah 49:7).
Possibly descended from Shuah, a son of Abraham and Keturah (Genesis 25:2).
From Naamah, a place of uncertain location.

chapters.n: Seeing him from a distance, they barely recognize him. They weep aloud, tear their robes, and throw dust in the air over their heads in mourning.

f.g: Did not recognize him.

chapters.n: They sit silently with him on the ground for seven days and nights. Their silent presence was their best comfort — later, their words will hurt more than help.

f.g: The traditional period of mourning for the dead (Genesis 50:10).

f.w: none spake a word unto him

chapters.n: After seven days of silence, Job finally speaks — and he curses the day he was born. Notice he does not curse God, as Satan predicted; he curses his own birthday.

f.g: Cursed his birthday, not God.

chapters.n: From here until chapter 42 the book shifts from prose story to Hebrew poetry. Job’s raw, honest lament begins.

f.g: Literally “answered” — responding to his situation.

chapters.n: Job wishes the day of his birth — and the night he was conceived — had never existed. The two lines use Hebrew parallelism: saying the same idea twice in different words.

f.g: A boy is conceived — announcing the start of his life.

chapters.n: He wishes that day would be wrapped in darkness, as if reversing God’s first creative word, “Let there be light.”

f.g: A reversal of Genesis 1:3, “Let there be light.”
Pay attention to, care about.

chapters.n: He piles up images of gloom — deep darkness, clouds, eclipse — hoping to blot that day out entirely.

f.g: Deep darkness, the thickest gloom (compare Psalms 23:4).
Literally “redeem” or “claim it back” — let darkness take it back.

chapters.n: Let that night be erased from the calendar, never counted among the days of the year.

f.w: let it not be joined unto the days of the year
f.g: Let it be removed from the calendar.

chapters.n: Let that night be barren and silent, with no joyful birth cry or celebration.

f.g: Barren, empty.

chapters.n: Job calls on those skilled in cursing — even those who can rouse the sea monster Leviathan — to curse that day. He uses ancient imagery of chaos.

f.g: The Hebrew reads “Leviathan,” a mythic sea monster symbolizing chaos (Job 41:1; Isaiah 27:1).

chapters.n: Let that night’s morning stars stay dark, waiting for a dawn that never comes.

f.g: Literally “the eyelids of the morning” — the first rays of dawn.

chapters.n: Why curse that day? Because it didn’t keep him from being born and seeing such sorrow.

f.w: shut not up the doors of my mother's womb
f.g: Didn’t prevent his birth.

chapters.n: Now Job asks “why?” — the first of many questions in the book. Why didn’t I die at birth?

f.g: Die, breathe my last.

chapters.n: Why was I received onto my mother’s knees and nursed? Why was I cared for at all?

f.g: In KJV English, “come before, receive” — the knees that received him at birth.

chapters.n: If he had died, he would now be resting peacefully. Job imagines death as quiet sleep, an escape from pain.

f.g: Death is often pictured as sleep in scripture (Daniel 12:2).

chapters.n: He would be resting with the kings and advisers of the past, whose grand buildings have now fallen into ruin. Death levels all human greatness.

f.g: Built monuments or tombs that now lie in ruins.

chapters.n: Or with wealthy princes whose silver-filled houses could not keep them from death.
Or he could have been like a stillborn child, never seeing the light of life at all.

f.g: A miscarried or stillborn baby.

chapters.n: In the grave, the wicked can no longer cause trouble, and the exhausted find rest. Job longs for that peace.

f.w: there the weary be at rest

chapters.n: Prisoners there are at ease, no longer hearing the shouts of their slave drivers.

f.g: The shout of the taskmaster.

chapters.n: In death, small and great are equal, and the slave is free from his master. Job sees death as a great equalizer.

f.w: The small and great are there

chapters.n: Job widens his question: why does God give life to people who only suffer? It is the cry of countless sufferers through history.

f.g: Deeply anguished.

chapters.n: They long for death, searching for it more eagerly than for buried treasure, yet it doesn’t come.

f.w: dig for it more than for hid treasures

chapters.n: They would rejoice to find the grave. This shows the depth of Job’s despair — honest feelings the book does not hide.

f.w: when they can find the grave
f.g: When they finally die.

chapters.n: Why give life to someone who can’t see a way forward, whom God has fenced in? Ironically, Satan had complained God put a protective hedge around Job; now Job feels hemmed in.

f.g: Who cannot see the path ahead.

chapters.n: His groans come in place of food, and his cries pour out like water.

f.w: my sighing cometh before I eat
f.g: Groaning has become his daily bread.
Loud groans of anguish (Psalms 22:1).

chapters.n: The very thing he feared most has happened. Even in prosperity, Job may have worried about losing it all — and now he has.

f.w: the thing which I greatly feared
f.g: His worst fears have come true.

chapters.n: He has no peace, no quiet, no rest — only trouble. The chapter ends without resolution, setting up the long debate with his friends.

f.g: Literally “turmoil came” — the same word used for anger or agitation.

chapters.n: Eliphaz, probably the oldest of the friends, speaks first. This begins three rounds of speeches between Job and his friends (chapters 4–27). Keep in mind that at the end God says the friends did not speak rightly about Him (Job 42:7).
He begins politely: Will you be upset if we speak? But I can’t keep quiet.

f.g: Try to speak.
Hold himself back.

chapters.n: Eliphaz reminds Job that he once taught and strengthened many weak people.
Job’s words used to lift up the stumbling and steady trembling knees. This image is echoed later in scripture as a call to serve.
Now that trouble has hit Job himself, Eliphaz says, he falls apart. It’s a gentle jab: you could give advice, but can you take it?

f.g: Lose heart, become discouraged.

chapters.n: Shouldn’t your reverence for God and your upright life give you confidence and hope? Eliphaz assumes a righteous person has nothing to fear.

f.g: Your reverence for God.

chapters.n: Here is Eliphaz’s core belief: innocent people never perish; only the wicked are destroyed. The book of Job challenges this simple formula — and so does the life of Jesus, the innocent One who suffered.

f.g: The friends’ view: suffering always proves sin. The book as a whole rejects this.

chapters.n: From his experience, those who plant evil harvest evil. That is a true principle in general — but Eliphaz wrongly applies it to every case of suffering.
The wicked are destroyed by a blast of God’s breath, like plants withered by a hot wind.
Eliphaz compares the wicked to fierce lions whose roar is silenced and teeth are broken. Five different Hebrew words for “lion” are used in verses 10–11.

f.g: Hebrew has many words for lions; this poem uses five of them.

chapters.n: Even strong lions die without prey, and their cubs scatter. The wicked, however powerful, eventually fall.

f.g: Cubs.

chapters.n: Eliphaz claims a secret revelation — a message whispered to him.

f.g: Stealthily revealed to me.
A whisper.

chapters.n: It came in disturbing night visions, during deep sleep.

f.g: The same word used of Adam’s and Abram’s deep sleep (Genesis 2:21; 15:12).

chapters.n: He was seized by fear and trembling until his bones shook.

f.w: made all my bones to shake
f.g: Terrified him to the core.

chapters.n: A spirit or breath of wind passed by his face, and his hair stood on end. The scene is eerie and mysterious.

f.g: Hebrew ruach — can mean spirit, wind, or breath.

chapters.n: A shadowy form stood before him in silence, and then he heard a voice. It is an unsettling vision — and we may wonder whether its source was truly divine.

f.w: there was silence, and I heard a voice

chapters.n: The message: Can a mortal be more righteous than God, or purer than his Maker? It is true in itself, but Eliphaz uses it to imply Job must be guilty.

f.w: Shall mortal man be more just than God?

chapters.n: Even God’s heavenly servants and angels can’t be fully trusted by Him, the vision says, and He charges them with error.

f.g: Found fault with, accused of error.

chapters.n: How much less can He trust humans, living in fragile bodies of clay, who can be crushed as easily as a moth.

f.g: Mortal bodies made from the dust (Genesis 2:7; 2 Corinthians 5:1).
Crushed as easily as a moth.

chapters.n: Human life is fragile: between morning and evening people die, and they vanish without anyone noticing.

f.g: Without anyone paying attention.

chapters.n: Their life is pulled up like a tent cord, and they die without ever gaining wisdom. Eliphaz’s point: humble yourself, Job, for you are mortal and flawed.

f.w: their excellency which is in them go away
f.g: Many translate it “their tent cord is pulled up” — an image of death.
Without having understood life.

chapters.n: Eliphaz continues: Go ahead and call out — will any heavenly being take your side? He suggests no one in heaven will support Job’s complaint.

f.g: “Holy ones” — heavenly beings or angels.

chapters.n: Resentment destroys the fool. Eliphaz hints that Job’s angry lament is the kind of thing that ruins a person.

f.g: The simple or naive person.

chapters.n: Eliphaz has seen fools seem to prosper and put down roots, but he pronounced their home cursed, and it soon fell.

f.g: Home, dwelling.

chapters.n: The fool’s children find no safety and are crushed in court with no one to defend them. These words would wound Job, whose children had just died.

f.g: Defeated in court — legal cases were heard at the city gate.

chapters.n: The hungry eat the fool’s harvest, even taking it from among thorns, and thieves swallow his wealth — another painful echo of Job’s recent losses.

f.g: Wealth, possessions.

chapters.n: Trouble doesn’t just sprout from the ground like weeds — it has a cause.

f.w: cometh not forth of the dust
f.g: Doesn’t arise by itself, without a reason.

chapters.n: Human beings are born to trouble as surely as sparks fly upward from a fire. This famous line has been quoted for centuries as a description of mortal life.

f.g: Literally “sons of Resheph” — sparks or flames flying up.

chapters.n: Eliphaz’s advice: If I were you, I would turn to God and bring my case to Him. Good counsel — though Job will indeed do so, more boldly than Eliphaz expects.
God does great and unsearchable things, wonders beyond counting.

f.g: Beyond human understanding.

chapters.n: He sends rain to water the earth and the fields — a life-giving gift in a dry land.

f.w: Who giveth rain upon the earth

chapters.n: He lifts up the lowly and brings those who mourn to safety. God reverses fortunes — a theme also seen in Hannah’s and Mary’s songs.

f.w: To set up on high those that be low

chapters.n: God frustrates the schemes of clever plotters so they cannot succeed.

f.w: disappointeth the devices of the crafty

chapters.n: He catches the wise in their own cleverness. Paul quotes this line in the New Testament — the only time Job is quoted there.

f.w: He taketh the wise in their own craftiness

f.g: Perverse, crooked, stubborn.

chapters.n: The schemers stumble around in broad daylight as if it were night — confused and lost.
God rescues the poor from the sword of cruel words and from the hands of the powerful.

f.g: From the “sword” of their slanderous mouths.

chapters.n: So the poor have hope, and injustice is silenced.
Eliphaz now offers a true principle: blessed is the one God corrects, so don’t reject His discipline. But he assumes Job’s suffering must be correction for sin.

f.w: happy is the man whom God correcteth

f.g: Discipline, correction.
Hebrew Shaddai, a name for God used often in Job.

chapters.n: God wounds, but He also binds up; He strikes, and His hands heal. A beautiful truth about God’s healing power.

f.w: he woundeth, and his hands make whole

chapters.n: “Six troubles, yea, seven” is a Hebrew number pattern meaning “every trouble.” God will protect you in all of them.

f.w: in six troubles: yea, in seven
f.g: A Hebrew way of saying “in every possible trouble.”

chapters.n: In famine and in war, God will save you from death.

f.g: Rescue, buy back.

chapters.n: He will protect you from slander and from fear of disaster.

f.g: The whip of slander and gossip.

chapters.n: You will even laugh at destruction and famine and not fear wild animals. Eliphaz paints a picture of perfect security.

f.g: Be unafraid, confident.

chapters.n: You will be at peace with the stones of the field — they won’t ruin your crops — and wild animals will live peacefully with you. It is an image of creation in harmony.

f.w: in league with the stones of the field
f.g: Your fields will be free of stones that ruin farming.

f.w: the beasts of the field shall be at peace with thee

chapters.n: Your home will be safe, and when you check your flocks, nothing will be missing.

f.g: Tent, home.
Here likely meaning “shall miss nothing” — find nothing lacking.

chapters.n: Your children will be many, like the grass of the earth. To a man who had just buried ten children, this promise must have stung.

f.w: thine offspring as the grass of the earth

chapters.n: You will reach the grave in ripe old age, like a sheaf of grain gathered at harvest time. Ironically, this does come true for Job in the end (Job 42:16-17).

f.g: A bundle of harvested grain stalks.

f.w: Thou shalt come to thy grave in a full age

chapters.n: Eliphaz concludes confidently: we have studied this, and it is true — accept it for your own good. His sincere but rigid theology leaves no room for innocent suffering.

f.g: We have investigated it thoroughly.

chapters.n: Job responds to Eliphaz. Instead of arguing theology, he first asks his friends to understand how much he hurts.

f.g: Job replies to Eliphaz’s speech in chapters 4–5.

chapters.n: If only someone could weigh my grief and my disaster on a scale!

f.g: Thoroughly.
A set of scales for weighing.

chapters.n: His sorrow would outweigh all the sand of the sea — that’s why his words have been wild. Job admits his speech was rash, but asks them to understand why.

f.g: My words have been rash or reckless.

f.w: heavier than the sand of the sea

chapters.n: Job feels that God Himself has shot poisoned arrows into him, and terrors from God are lined up against him like an army. He doesn’t know about the heavenly scene in chapters 1–2.

f.g: Line up for battle.

chapters.n: Animals don’t complain when they have food. Job’s point: he wouldn’t be crying out if he weren’t truly suffering.

f.g: Moos.
Animal feed.

chapters.n: Who can eat bland food without salt, or enjoy the taste of egg white? Eliphaz’s advice tastes just as flat to Job.

f.g: Tasteless.
The Hebrew is uncertain; some think it means the juice of a bland plant.

chapters.n: What he once refused to touch has become his miserable diet — his suffering, or perhaps his friends’ counsel, makes him sick.

f.g: Food.

chapters.n: Job has one request he longs for God to grant.

f.w: Oh that I might have my request
f.g: A deep wish, often introduced this way in Job.

chapters.n: His wish is that God would just end his life — cut the thread of his life like a weaver cuts cloth from the loom.

f.g: Literally cut off like thread from a loom (compare Isaiah 38:12).

chapters.n: That would still be a comfort: he could leap for joy even in pain, knowing he never denied the words of the Holy One. Job holds on to his integrity.

f.g: Possibly “leap for joy” or “exult” — the Hebrew is uncertain.

f.w: I have not concealed the words of the Holy One
f.g: I have not denied or rejected God’s words.

chapters.n: Job feels he has no strength left to keep hoping and no future worth waiting for.

f.g: What future do I have?

chapters.n: He is not made of stone or bronze. Human endurance has limits.

f.g: Bronze.

chapters.n: He feels he has no inner resources left; any success has been driven away from him.

f.g: Here possibly “success” or “resourcefulness.”

chapters.n: A suffering person should receive loyal kindness from a friend — even if he were to abandon the fear of God. Friendship should not depend on agreement.

f.g: Hebrew hesed — loyal, steadfast kindness.

f.w: To him that is afflicted pity should be shewed

chapters.n: Job compares his friends to desert streams: full when there’s no need, dry when you need water. Their friendship has proven unreliable.

f.g: Like a wadi — a seasonal stream that disappears in summer.

chapters.n: In winter these streams run dark with melting ice and snow.

f.g: Dark, murky.

chapters.n: But when the heat comes, they vanish. When travelers most need them, they are gone.
Caravans turn off their route to find water, but the stream has disappeared, and they wander into the desert and die.

f.w: The paths of their way are turned aside
f.g: Caravans leave the road looking for water.

chapters.n: Caravans from Tema and Sheba, Arabian trading peoples, look hopefully for the water.

f.g: An oasis town in northwest Arabia.
A trading kingdom in southern Arabia.

chapters.n: Their hopes are crushed; they arrive to find nothing and are put to shame.

f.g: Bewildered, disappointed.

chapters.n: So it is with you, Job says: you see my horrible condition and pull back in fear. Perhaps they feared that whatever struck Job could strike them.

f.w: ye see my casting down, and are afraid
f.g: You see my disaster and draw back in fear.

chapters.n: Did I ask you for money or gifts? Job had asked nothing of them except understanding.

f.g: Wealth.

chapters.n: Did I ask you to rescue me from enemies or pay a ransom? No — only for compassion.

f.g: Buy back, ransom.

chapters.n: Job challenges them honestly: Teach me and I’ll be quiet. Show me where I went wrong.

f.w: cause me to understand wherein I have erred

chapters.n: Honest words are powerful — but your arguments prove nothing.

f.g: How painful (or how powerful) honest words can be.
Correct, prove wrong.

chapters.n: Do you mean to criticize my words? A desperate man’s words are like the wind — don’t hold them against him.

f.g: Empty, passing — not to be taken too seriously.

chapters.n: You would even gamble over an orphan and sell out your friend. Job feels betrayed.

f.g: Literally “cast lots over the orphan” — treat the helpless heartlessly.

f.w: dig a pit for your friend
f.g: Possibly “bargain over your friend.”

chapters.n: Look me in the face — would I lie to you? Job pleads to be heard as a person, not as a theological case.

f.g: Be willing; please.

chapters.n: Turn back and reconsider — don’t be unjust. My integrity is still at stake.

f.g: Change your mind, reconsider.
My innocence is on the line.

chapters.n: Is there anything false in my words? Can’t I tell right from wrong? Job insists his conscience is clear.

f.w: cannot my taste discern perverse things?
f.g: Can’t I tell what is evil or wrong?

chapters.n: Job compares human life to hard military service or the life of a hired laborer — long, tiring, and under someone else’s control.

f.g: Literally “hard service,” like a soldier’s term of duty.
A hired day laborer.

chapters.n: Like a slave longing for evening shade or a worker waiting for his wages, Job longs for relief.

f.g: The shade of evening, when work ends.

chapters.n: Instead, he has been given months of emptiness and nights of misery.

f.g: Emptiness, futility.

chapters.n: At night he can’t sleep, tossing and turning until dawn, wishing the night would end. Anyone who has suffered sleepless nights will recognize this.

f.g: Restless turning in bed.

chapters.n: His body is covered with worms and scabs; his skin cracks and oozes. Job describes his disease in painful detail.

f.g: Crusty scabs.
Running with pus; disgusting.

chapters.n: His days fly by faster than a weaver’s shuttle, and they run out without hope. In Hebrew, “hope” can also mean “thread” — his life is ending like a thread run out.

f.g: The tool that carries thread quickly back and forth on a loom.
A wordplay: Hebrew tiqvah means both “hope” and “thread.”

chapters.n: Job now speaks directly to God: remember that my life is just a breath; I’ll never see good again.
Soon no one will see him again. “You will look for me, but I will be gone.”

f.w: thine eyes are upon me, and I am not
f.g: You will look for me, but I will no longer exist.

chapters.n: Like a cloud that disappears, someone who goes down to the grave does not come back up. At this low point Job sees no hope beyond death; later he will reach toward a hope of resurrection (Job 14:14; 19:25-26).

f.g: Hebrew Sheol — the world of the dead.

chapters.n: He will never return home, and his own house will forget him.

f.w: neither shall his place know him any more

chapters.n: So Job won’t hold back. He will speak out of the anguish and bitterness of his soul. His honest complaint is itself a kind of prayer.

f.w: I will not refrain my mouth

chapters.n: Am I the raging sea or a sea monster that you must keep me under guard? In ancient imagery, the sea and its monsters were forces of chaos that God restrained.

f.g: Hebrew tannin — a sea monster or dragon, symbol of chaos.

chapters.n: When he hopes his bed will give him some comfort...
...God terrifies him with nightmares and visions. Even sleep offers no escape.

f.g: Frightens me with nightmares.

chapters.n: He would rather be strangled than continue living like this.

f.g: Suffocation, death.

chapters.n: I hate my life; I don’t want to live forever. Leave me alone — my days are only a breath.

f.g: I don’t want to live forever.
A breath, vapor — fleeting.

chapters.n: Job twists the words of Psalm 8. The psalmist marveled that God cares for mankind; Job asks why God pays so much attention to him — it feels like scrutiny, not love.

f.w: What is man, that thou shouldest magnify him?

chapters.n: Why inspect him every morning and test him every moment? Job feels constantly examined.

f.g: Inspect, examine.
Test.

chapters.n: How long until you look away and let me alone even long enough to swallow? A vivid Hebrew idiom for “just a moment’s break.”

f.w: till I swallow down my spittle
f.g: An idiom: not even a moment’s rest.

chapters.n: Even if I have sinned, what have I done to you, you watcher of humankind? Why make me your target? Job does not admit guilt, but asks why any sin of his would matter so much.

f.g: Literally “watcher of men” — here with a bitter edge.
A target.

chapters.n: Why not just forgive me? Soon I will lie in the dust; you will look for me and I’ll be gone. Even in his complaint, Job assumes God would miss him — a glimmer of the relationship he still believes in.

f.w: why dost thou not pardon my transgression
thou shalt seek me in the morning
f.g: Job imagines God searching for him after he dies.

chapters.n: The second friend, Bildad, now speaks. He is blunter than Eliphaz and relies on the wisdom of tradition.
He opens impatiently: How long will you go on? Your words are just a blast of hot air.

f.g: Loud but empty, blustering.

chapters.n: Bildad’s central question: Does God ever twist justice? Of course not. But he assumes that means Job’s suffering must be deserved.

f.g: Distort justice.

chapters.n: With painful cruelty, Bildad suggests Job’s children died because they sinned. He turns theology into a weapon against a grieving father.

f.w: cast them away for their transgression
f.g: Literally “gave them into the hand of their transgression.”

chapters.n: If you would earnestly seek God and plead with Him...

f.g: Early, earnestly, diligently.
Humble pleading.

chapters.n: ...and if you are truly pure and upright, God would rouse Himself for you and restore your rightful home. The “if” implies Bildad doubts Job’s innocence.

f.g: He would rise up to act on your behalf.

chapters.n: Your beginning would seem small compared to your future greatness. Ironically, this comes true in Job 42 — but not for the reasons Bildad thinks.

f.w: thy latter end should greatly increase

chapters.n: Bildad appeals to tradition: ask earlier generations and learn what their fathers discovered.

f.g: Previous generations.

chapters.n: We were born only yesterday and know nothing; our lives are as fleeting as a shadow.

f.w: our days upon earth are a shadow

chapters.n: The ancients will teach you from their deep understanding. Tradition can carry real wisdom — but it can also be misapplied.

f.g: From their understanding.

chapters.n: Can papyrus grow without a marsh, or reeds without water? Bildad begins a nature lesson.

f.g: Papyrus, a tall water plant.
A reed or marsh grass.
Marshy mud.

chapters.n: Cut off from water, such plants wither even while green, faster than other plants.

f.g: Its freshness, still in full growth.

chapters.n: So it is with those who forget God: their hope dies. Bildad implies Job is godless.

f.g: Hebrew “the godless person’s hope.”

chapters.n: Their confidence is as fragile as a spider’s web.
He leans on his house, but it collapses; he grabs hold, but it won’t hold. Trusting in anything but God gives way.

f.w: He shall lean upon his house

chapters.n: Bildad shifts to a new picture: a well-watered plant thriving in the sun, spreading through the garden.

f.g: Flourishing in the sunlight.

chapters.n: Its roots wrap around rocks and grip the stones. It seems secure.

f.g: A pile of stones.

chapters.n: But once it is torn out, its place denies ever knowing it. The wicked vanish without a trace.
That’s the “joy” of the wicked — short-lived — and other plants spring up in its place. Bildad’s tone is mocking.

f.g: Said ironically — this is all his “happiness” amounts to.

chapters.n: God won’t reject a blameless person or help evildoers. Bildad uses the same word that described Job in chapter 1 — “perfect” — without realizing it fits Job exactly.
He will yet fill your mouth with laughter and your lips with shouts of joy. A hopeful promise, though offered on a condition.
Your enemies will be covered with shame, and the tents of the wicked will disappear. Bildad means well at the end, but his view leaves no room for innocent suffering.

f.g: Disappear, come to nothing.

chapters.n: Job answers Bildad, but much of this speech is really about how to stand before God.

f.g: Job’s reply to Bildad (chapter 8).

chapters.n: Yes, I know God is just. But how can any human be declared right before God? Job uses the language of a courtroom, a theme that runs through the book.

f.w: how should man be just with God?
f.g: How can a person win a legal case against God, or be declared innocent?

chapters.n: If someone tried to argue with God, he couldn’t answer even one question in a thousand.

f.g: Argue a legal case.

chapters.n: God is all-wise and all-powerful. Who has ever defied Him and come out unharmed?

f.g: Stubbornly resisted.

chapters.n: Job praises God’s power in a hymn-like passage (verses 5–10). God moves mountains before they know it and overturns them in His anger.

f.g: Without their realizing it — suddenly.

chapters.n: He shakes the earth from its place, and its foundations tremble — a picture of earthquakes.

f.g: Ancient poetic image of the earth resting on pillars (1 Samuel 2:8).

chapters.n: He can command the sun not to rise and seal up the stars so they don’t shine.

f.g: Hides them from view.

chapters.n: God alone stretched out the heavens and walks on the waves of the sea. Christians may think of Jesus walking on the water.

f.w: treadeth upon the waves of the sea

chapters.n: He made the great constellations. Ancient people watched these star groups to mark the seasons.

f.g: Probably the Great Bear (Big Dipper); the exact identification is uncertain.
Constellations of the southern sky.

chapters.n: He does great things beyond understanding, wonders without number. Job repeats Eliphaz’s words (Job 5:9), but with a darker tone.
God passes right by, yet Job can’t see Him. He feels God is near but hidden — a common experience in suffering.

f.w: he goeth by me, and I see him not

chapters.n: If God takes something away, who can stop Him or question Him?
God doesn’t hold back His anger; even the helpers of Rahab bow beneath Him. Rahab here is a mythic sea monster, a symbol of chaos — not the woman of Jericho.

f.g: Hebrew “helpers of Rahab,” a mythic chaos monster God defeated (Isaiah 51:9).

chapters.n: How then could I possibly answer Him or find the right words to argue my case?
Even if I were innocent, I couldn’t answer; I could only beg my judge for mercy.

f.g: Plea for mercy.

chapters.n: Even if He answered me, I wouldn’t believe He was really listening. Job’s trust is badly shaken.

f.g: Listened.

chapters.n: He crushes me with a storm and multiplies my wounds for no reason. Job doesn’t know it, but the narrator agrees — the suffering truly was “without cause” (Job 2:3).

f.g: Storm, whirlwind.

chapters.n: He won’t even let me catch my breath, but fills me with bitterness.

f.g: Allow.

chapters.n: If it’s a matter of strength, He is strong. If it’s a matter of justice, who can summon Him to court?

f.w: set me a time to plead
f.g: Summon Him to a court hearing.

chapters.n: If I declare myself right, my own words would seem to condemn me. In an unequal contest, even innocence can’t be proven.

f.g: Crooked, guilty.

chapters.n: I am blameless, Job says — but I no longer care about myself; I loathe my life.

f.g: Better: “I am blameless.”

f.w: yet would I not know my soul
f.g: I don’t care about myself anymore.

chapters.n: It’s all the same, Job says: God destroys both the blameless and the wicked. He is wrestling with the fact that suffering seems to strike good and bad alike.

f.w: He destroyeth the perfect and the wicked

chapters.n: When disaster brings sudden death, God seems to mock the despair of the innocent. These are the words of a man in anguish, not a settled doctrine.

f.g: Whip — a sudden disaster.

chapters.n: The world seems handed over to the wicked, and judges are blindfolded. If God isn’t responsible, then who is?

f.w: covereth the faces of the judges
f.g: Blinds judges so they can’t see justice.

chapters.n: Job’s days race by faster than a royal courier and see nothing good.

f.g: A swift runner carrying messages.

chapters.n: They pass like fast papyrus boats or an eagle swooping on its prey.

f.g: Light boats made of papyrus reeds.

chapters.n: If Job tries to forget his complaint and put on a cheerful face...

f.g: Stop looking sad.

chapters.n: ...he still dreads his suffering, sure that God will not declare him innocent.

f.g: Acquit me.

chapters.n: If I’m already judged guilty, why bother trying?

f.g: Struggle uselessly.

chapters.n: Even if he washed with snow and cleansed his hands with soap...

f.w: make my hands never so clean
f.g: Literally “cleanse my hands with lye” — strong soap.

chapters.n: ...God would plunge him into a filthy pit, so that even his own clothes would be disgusted by him. Job feels no effort could make him clean before God.

f.g: A pit of filth.
Detest.

chapters.n: God is not a man like me, Job says, that we could meet as equals in court.

f.w: he is not a man, as I am

chapters.n: Job longs for a “daysman” — an umpire who could put one hand on God and one on Job and bring them together. Christians see this longing answered in Jesus Christ, the Mediator who is both God and man.

f.g: An umpire or mediator — one who sets a day for a hearing and judges between two parties.

f.w: lay his hand upon us both

chapters.n: If only God would take away His rod and stop terrifying him!

f.g: His staff of punishment.

chapters.n: Then Job could speak without fear. But as things are, he cannot. The chapter ends with Job still longing to meet God face to face.

f.w: but it is not so with me
f.g: But that’s not my situation.

chapters.n: Job is tired of living, so he will let his complaint flow freely and speak from his bitterness. This whole chapter is addressed to God — raw, honest prayer.

f.w: I will leave my complaint upon myself
f.g: I will give free rein to my complaint.

f.w: My soul is weary of my life

chapters.n: He asks God not to simply condemn him, but to show him the charges. Job wants to know why he is suffering.

f.w: shew me wherefore thou contendest with me
f.g: Tell me what charge you have against me.

chapters.n: Does it please you, God, to crush the work of your own hands while smiling on the plans of the wicked? Job appeals to God as his Creator.
Do you see with human eyes, limited and easily fooled? Job knows God sees perfectly — so why treat him as a suspect?

f.g: Human, limited vision.

chapters.n: Is your life short like a human’s, so you must rush to find fault before time runs out?
Why then do you search so hard for my sin?
You know I’m not guilty, yet no one can rescue me from your power. Job is confident in his innocence but feels trapped.

f.w: Thou knowest that I am not wicked

chapters.n: Your hands shaped me with care — and now you would destroy me? It doesn’t make sense to Job that a loving Creator would ruin His own work.

f.g: Shaped me completely, all over.

chapters.n: Remember that you made me from clay. Will you now turn me back to dust?
Job describes his formation in the womb in poetic language: like milk poured out and thickened into cheese.

f.g: An ancient image of how a body takes shape in the womb.

chapters.n: God clothed him with skin and flesh and knit him together with bones and sinews. Compare the wonder of Psalm 139.

f.w: fenced me with bones and sinews
f.g: Wove me together with bones and tendons.

f.w: clothed me with skin and flesh

chapters.n: You gave me life and showed me steadfast love, and your care watched over my spirit. Job remembers God’s past goodness.

f.g: Hebrew hesed — loyal, covenant love.
Your watchful care.

chapters.n: But now Job suspects God had a hidden purpose all along — to watch for his faults. In a deeper sense, God did have a hidden purpose, as the reader knows from chapters 1–2.

f.g: Kept secretly in mind.

chapters.n: If I sin, you watch me and won’t forgive me.

f.g: Watch closely, keep record.
Declare innocent.

chapters.n: If I’m guilty, I’m doomed; if I’m innocent, I still can’t lift my head in honor. I am filled with shame — look at my misery.

f.w: yet will I not lift up my head
f.g: I can’t hold my head up — I’m covered in shame.
Filled with disgrace.

chapters.n: If I lift my head, you hunt me like a lion and again show your awesome power against me.

f.w: Thou huntest me as a fierce lion

chapters.n: You keep bringing new witnesses against me and increase your anger; wave after wave of troubles attacks me.

f.g: Perhaps his sores and losses, which seem to “testify” against him.
Wave after wave of attacking forces.

chapters.n: Why did you let me be born? I wish I had died before anyone saw me. Job returns to the lament of chapter 3.

f.w: Wherefore then hast thou brought me forth out of the womb?

chapters.n: It would have been better never to have existed — carried straight from the womb to the grave.
My life is short; just leave me alone so I can have a little comfort.

f.g: Brighten up a little; find a moment of cheer.

chapters.n: ...before I go to the place from which I won’t return — the land of darkness and deep shadow.

f.g: Deep darkness (compare Psalms 23:4).

chapters.n: Job pictures the realm of the dead as a land of gloom and chaos, where even the light is dark. He has not yet seen the fuller light that later revelation brings about life after death.

f.g: Chaotic, without structure.

f.w: where the light is as darkness

chapters.n: The third friend, Zophar, speaks for the first time. He is the harshest of the three.
Should all this talk go unanswered? Should a big talker be proven right just by talking? Zophar dismisses Job’s pain as mere words.

f.g: Literally “a man of lips” — a windbag.

chapters.n: Should your empty boasting silence everyone? When you mock, shouldn’t someone shame you?

f.g: Better, “your idle talk” or “babble.”

chapters.n: Zophar summarizes Job’s claim: “My teaching is pure, and I am clean in your sight.” Job did insist on his innocence, but not that he had never sinned at all.

f.g: My teaching or understanding is sound.

chapters.n: Zophar wishes God would speak against Job. Ironically, God does speak at the end — and rebukes the friends instead (Job 42:7).
If only God would show you how deep His wisdom is! Then you’d know God is punishing you less than you deserve. This is Zophar’s cruelest line.

f.g: Many-sided, with layers of meaning.

f.w: exacteth of thee less than thine iniquity deserveth

chapters.n: Can you discover the depths of God by searching? Can you reach the limits of the Almighty? A true principle — God is beyond full human understanding.

f.w: Canst thou by searching find out God?

chapters.n: God’s wisdom is higher than the heavens and deeper than the underworld — beyond our reach.

f.g: Hebrew Sheol — the realm of the dead, here meaning the deepest depths.

chapters.n: It is longer than the earth and wider than the sea.
If God arrests someone and calls him to judgment, who can stop Him?

f.g: Pass by, imprison, or arrest.
Call to court.

chapters.n: God knows deceitful people; when He sees evil, He takes note. Zophar implies God has seen Job’s hidden sins.

f.g: Worthless or false people.

chapters.n: A proverb: a foolish person will become wise when a wild donkey is born human — in other words, never. It is an insult aimed at Job.

f.w: born like a wild ass's colt
f.g: A saying: an empty-headed man will gain sense when a wild donkey is born a man.

chapters.n: Zophar’s counsel: set your heart right and reach out your hands to God in prayer.

f.g: Raise your hands in prayer.

chapters.n: If there is sin in your hand, put it away, and don’t let evil live in your home. Good advice for repentance — though wrongly assuming Job is guilty.

f.g: Tents, home.

chapters.n: Then you could lift your face without shame, stand firm, and not be afraid.

f.g: Without blemish or shame.

chapters.n: You would forget your misery, remembering it like water that has flowed away.
Your life would shine brighter than noon; even darkness would become like morning.
You would feel secure because there is hope; you would look around and rest in safety.

f.g: Possibly “look around” or “search” — you would find all safe.

chapters.n: You would lie down without fear, and many would come seeking your favor. Indeed, in the end Job does pray for these very friends (Job 42:8-10).

f.g: Seek your favor.

f.w: many shall make suit unto thee

chapters.n: But the wicked will lose all hope; their only hope is their last breath. A final warning shot at Job.

f.w: the eyes of the wicked shall fail
f.g: They will look for help in vain.

f.w: the giving up of the ghost
f.g: Breathing one’s last — death.

chapters.n: Job begins his longest reply yet (chapters 12–14), answering all three friends.

f.g: Job’s response closes the first round of speeches.

chapters.n: He opens with sarcasm: Surely you are the only people who matter, and wisdom will die when you do!

f.g: Biting sarcasm at their know-it-all attitude.

chapters.n: I understand as much as you do. Everyone knows the things you’ve said — they’re common knowledge, not special insight.

f.w: I am not inferior to you

chapters.n: Job has become a joke to his friends — a righteous man who once prayed and was answered, now laughed at.

f.g: Mocked, ridiculed.

chapters.n: Those who are comfortable look down on people who are slipping. It’s easy to scorn trouble when you’re not in it.

f.g: The Hebrew may mean “contempt for misfortune” — the comfortable look down on the struggling.
Comfortable, carefree.

chapters.n: Meanwhile robbers’ homes thrive, and those who provoke God live securely. Job points out that real life doesn’t fit the friends’ neat theory.
Ask the animals and birds — they will teach you.

f.g: Nature itself shows that God controls all things, good and hard.

chapters.n: Ask the earth and the fish of the sea — they will tell you too.
All creation knows the Lord’s hand has done this. Interestingly, this is the only place in Job’s dialogues where the personal name “the LORD” (Jehovah) is used.

f.w: the hand of the LORD hath wrought this

f.g: Jehovah (YHWH) — used only here in the poetic dialogues of chapters 3–37.

chapters.n: Every living creature’s life and every human breath is in God’s hand.
Just as the tongue tastes food, the ear tests words. Job will judge his friends’ arguments for himself.

f.w: Doth not the ear try words?

f.g: Food.

chapters.n: Wisdom is supposed to come with age, they say. Job may be quoting their own claim — Bildad appealed to the elders (Job 8:8).

f.g: Possibly a quoted proverb that Job goes on to challenge.

chapters.n: But true wisdom and power belong to God. Job now begins his own hymn to God’s power (verses 13–25).

f.w: With him is wisdom and strength

chapters.n: What God tears down cannot be rebuilt; whom He imprisons cannot be freed.

f.g: Imprisons.

chapters.n: He holds back rain and there is drought; He sends water and there are floods.
Power and wisdom are His; both the deceiver and the deceived are under His control. Nothing is outside His reach.

f.w: the deceived and the deceiver are his
f.g: Both the one led astray and the one who misleads are under God’s rule.

chapters.n: God strips advisers of their power and makes judges look foolish. The rest of this hymn shows God humbling the proud.

f.g: Stripped, barefoot — led away as captives.

chapters.n: He removes the authority of kings and binds them like prisoners.

f.g: Strips kings of their authority.

f.w: girdeth their loins with a girdle
f.g: Ties a rope around them like captives.

chapters.n: He leads priests or princes away stripped and overthrows the powerful.

f.g: Hebrew can mean “priests.”

chapters.n: He silences trusted advisers and takes away the judgment of elders — undercutting the friends’ appeal to the wisdom of the aged.
He pours contempt on nobles and weakens the strong.

f.w: weakeneth the strength of the mighty
f.g: Literally “loosens the belt of the strong.”

chapters.n: He brings hidden things out of darkness into the light. Nothing is hidden from God.

f.g: Uncovers, reveals.

f.w: He discovereth deep things out of darkness

chapters.n: He makes nations great and then destroys them, expands them and then scatters them. History is in His hands.

f.g: Narrows, confines — or leads away into exile.

chapters.n: He takes away the sense of the world’s leaders and makes them wander in a trackless wasteland.

f.g: Takes away their understanding.

f.w: a wilderness where there is no way

chapters.n: They grope in the dark and stagger like drunkards. Job agrees God is all-powerful — his question is not whether God rules, but why He allows the righteous to suffer.
Job continues: I’ve seen and heard everything you’ve described about God’s power. I understand it.

f.w: mine eye hath seen all this
f.g: Referring to his description of God’s power in chapter 12.

chapters.n: Whatever you know, I know too. I’m not beneath you.

f.w: I am not inferior unto you

chapters.n: But Job doesn’t want to argue with his friends — he wants to speak directly to God and make his case. This is a bold act of faith: he still believes God will listen.

f.w: I desire to reason with God

chapters.n: You smear me with lies; you’re all worthless doctors. Their “medicine” only makes him worse.

f.g: Those who plaster over truth with falsehood.
Useless healers.

chapters.n: If only you would be completely silent — that would be the wisest thing you could do! Their seven days of silence (Job 2:13) was their best counsel.
Now listen to my argument and pay attention to my case.

f.g: Legal arguments.

chapters.n: Will you lie to defend God? Job makes a deep point: God doesn’t need to be defended with falsehoods.

f.w: Will ye speak wickedly for God?
f.g: Defending God with untruths dishonors Him.

chapters.n: Will you show favoritism to God, acting as His lawyers? God does not need biased advocates.

f.g: Show partiality, take sides unfairly.

chapters.n: Would it go well if God examined you? Can you fool Him as you might fool a man?

f.g: Examine you closely.

chapters.n: God will surely rebuke you if you secretly show partiality. This comes true at the end of the book, when God rebukes the friends (Job 42:7).
Shouldn’t God’s majesty terrify you and fill you with dread?

f.g: His majesty.

chapters.n: Your memorable sayings are proverbs of ashes; your defenses are as weak as clay.

f.g: Maxims, memorable sayings.
Defenses (like shields or walls) made of clay — easily broken.

chapters.n: Be quiet so I can speak — come what may. Job is ready to accept whatever happens.

f.w: let come on me what will
f.g: Whatever the consequences.

chapters.n: Why should I risk my life? Two idioms for taking a great risk. Job knows challenging God is dangerous, but he is willing.

f.w: take my flesh in my teeth
f.g: An idiom for risking everything, like an animal carrying its prey.

f.w: put my life in mine hand

chapters.n: One of the great statements of faith in scripture: “Though he slay me, yet will I trust in him.” Even facing death, Job holds on to God — while still insisting on his own integrity.

f.w: Though he slay me, yet will I trust in him

f.g: Defend my conduct, argue my case.

chapters.n: Job believes God will be his salvation, because a godless person would never dare to come before Him. Approaching God at all is evidence of his sincerity.

f.w: He also shall be my salvation

f.g: A godless person.

chapters.n: Listen carefully to what I am about to say.

f.g: Statement, testimony.

chapters.n: I have prepared my case, and I know I will be found innocent. Job is confident in his integrity.

f.g: Prepared my legal case.
I will be declared in the right.

chapters.n: Who can bring charges against me? If someone could, I would fall silent and die.

f.g: Bring a case against me.
Die.

chapters.n: Turning to God, Job asks for just two things, so he can come before Him without hiding.

f.w: do not two things unto me
f.g: Grant me two requests (listed in verse 21).

chapters.n: First: take your hand of suffering off me. Second: stop terrifying me. Then he could face God.

f.w: Withdraw thine hand far from me

chapters.n: Then call me, and I’ll answer — or let me speak, and you answer me. Job asks for a real conversation with God.

f.w: Then call thou, and I will answer

chapters.n: How many sins have I committed? Show me my wrongdoing. Job honestly invites God to reveal anything he has done wrong.

f.w: make me to know my transgression

chapters.n: Why do you hide your face and treat me like an enemy? God’s silence hurts Job more than his sores. In Hebrew, “enemy” (oyev) sounds much like “Job” (Iyyov).

f.g: Hebrew oyev — a wordplay on Job’s name, Iyyov.

chapters.n: Will you frighten a leaf blown by the wind? Will you chase dry straw? Job feels weak and insignificant.

f.g: Dry stalks left after harvest.

chapters.n: You write bitter charges against me and make me pay for the sins of my youth. Job wonders if old mistakes are being held against him.
You put my feet in shackles and watch every step, even marking the soles of my feet. He feels like a closely guarded prisoner.

f.g: Wooden restraints for a prisoner’s feet.

f.w: settest a print upon the heels of my feet
f.g: Mark or trace my footprints — tracking every move.

chapters.n: Meanwhile, man wastes away like something rotten, like a moth-eaten garment. This verse leads into chapter 14’s reflection on human frailty.

f.w: as a garment that is moth eaten

chapters.n: Job reflects on the human condition: every person born of a woman lives only a short time, and that life is full of trouble. These words are often read at funerals.

f.g: A Hebrew way of saying “every mortal human.”

f.w: of few days, and full of trouble

chapters.n: We bloom like a flower and are cut down; we pass like a shadow and don’t last.

f.w: He cometh forth like a flower, and is cut down
he fleeth also as a shadow

chapters.n: And yet you fix your eyes on such a frail creature and drag me into court with you? Job wonders why God would scrutinize something so small.

f.w: open thine eyes upon such an one
f.g: Pay such close attention to so frail a being.

chapters.n: Who can bring something pure out of something impure? No one. Human beings cannot make themselves clean — only God can. Latter-day Saints see this need answered in the Atonement of Jesus Christ.

f.w: Who can bring a clean thing out of an unclean?

chapters.n: God has already set the length of each life — the number of months and the limits no one can pass.

f.g: Limits.

chapters.n: So look away and let him rest, Job pleads, until he finishes his day like a hired worker.

f.g: Complete, finish.

chapters.n: Job contrasts people with trees. A tree that is cut down still has hope — it can sprout again and grow new shoots.

f.w: there is hope of a tree

f.g: New shoot.

chapters.n: Even if its roots grow old and its stump dies in the ground...

f.g: Stump.

chapters.n: ...at the mere scent of water it buds and puts out branches like a young plant.

f.w: through the scent of water it will bud
f.g: A beautiful image: just a hint of water revives it.

chapters.n: But a man dies and lies still; he breathes his last — and where is he? Job asks the oldest human question.

f.g: Lies powerless, laid low.

chapters.n: Like water vanishing from a lake or a river drying up...

f.g: A river.

chapters.n: ...so a man lies down and doesn’t rise, not until the heavens are gone. Job’s words leave a door open: “till the heavens be no more.” Scripture later teaches that the dead will indeed awake at the resurrection.

f.w: till the heavens be no more
nor be raised out of their sleep

chapters.n: Job’s hope begins to rise: if only God would hide him in the grave until His anger passed, then set a time to remember him and bring him back!

f.g: Hebrew Sheol — the world of the dead.

chapters.n: The great question: “If a man die, shall he live again?” Job resolves to wait through his hard service until his “change” comes. Later he will testify, “I know that my redeemer liveth” (Job 19:25). Latter-day Saints affirm the answer through Christ’s resurrection.

f.w: If a man die, shall he live again?

f.g: Relief, release — like a soldier relieved at the end of his duty.

chapters.n: You will call, and I will answer; you will long for the creature your hands have made. Job glimpses a loving God who yearns for His children.

f.w: thou wilt have a desire to the work of thine hands

chapters.n: For now, though, God seems to count Job’s every step and keep watch over his sin.
Some read this as hope: God seals Job’s sins in a bag and covers them up — out of sight, as if forgiven. Others read it as God storing up evidence.

f.g: Possibly an image of sins put away and covered — forgiven (compare Micah 7:19).
Covers over, plasters over.

chapters.n: But then Job’s hope fades again. Even mountains crumble and rocks shift from their places.

f.g: Wears away, crumbles.

chapters.n: As water wears away stones and floods wash away soil, so God wears down human hope.

f.g: Slow erosion — a picture of gradual loss.

chapters.n: God overpowers a person forever; He changes his face in death and sends him away.

f.g: Changes his appearance — in death.

chapters.n: The dead don’t know whether their children rise to honor or fall into disgrace. Job, who lost all his children, feels this keenly.
He feels only his own pain and mourns only for himself. The chapter ends in sorrow — yet the question of verse 14 has been raised, and the book will return to it.

f.w: his soul within him shall mourn

chapters.n: Eliphaz, the oldest-sounding and most respected of Job’s three friends, begins his second speech. The friendly tone of his first speech (chapters 4–5) is gone.

f.g: From Teman in Edom, a region known for its wise men (Jeremiah 49:7).

chapters.n: Eliphaz mocks Job’s words as hot air. A truly wise man, he says, would not fill himself with empty talk like a stomach bloated with wind.

f.g: The scorching desert wind (the sirocco) — a picture of words that are hot, harsh, and useless.

chapters.n: He asks whether arguing with words that accomplish nothing is fitting for a wise man. To Eliphaz, Job’s complaints are not just wrong but pointless.

f.g: Speech that does no good to anyone.

chapters.n: Eliphaz claims Job’s complaints undermine reverence for God. If people talked like Job, he suggests, they would stop fearing God and stop praying.

f.g: Literally “diminish devotion” — you are weakening worship and meditation before God.

chapters.n: He argues that Job’s very words reveal hidden sin. The way Job speaks, Eliphaz says, is the clever, slippery speech of a guilty person.

f.g: Shrewd or cunning people; the same word describes the serpent in Genesis 3:1.

chapters.n: Eliphaz insists he doesn’t need to accuse Job — Job’s own mouth convicts him. It is a sharp turn from comforter to prosecutor.

f.w: thine own lips testify against thee

chapters.n: With sarcasm he asks whether Job thinks he is the first human ever born, older than the hills, and therefore wiser than everyone.

f.g: Language used of Wisdom herself in Proverbs — Eliphaz mocks Job for acting as if he were Wisdom personified.

chapters.n: Eliphaz asks whether Job has listened in on God’s private council and kept its wisdom to himself.

f.g: Hebrew sod — the intimate council of God. Compare Amos 3:7, where the Lord reveals his secret to his prophets.

chapters.n: He turns Job’s earlier words back on him (12:3; 13:2). Job claimed his friends knew nothing he did not; Eliphaz says the reverse.

f.w: What knowest thou, that we know not?

chapters.n: Eliphaz appeals to age and tradition: gray-haired elders, older even than Job’s father, stand on the friends’ side.

f.g: In the ancient Near East gray hair signaled wisdom and authority.

chapters.n: He asks whether Job thinks God’s comforts — perhaps meaning the friends’ gentle words — are too small for him. Eliphaz sees his own counsel as God’s consolation.

f.g: Probably Eliphaz’s own earlier, gentle speech, which he presents as comfort from God.

chapters.n: Eliphaz asks why Job lets his emotions run away with him and why his eyes flash with anger.

f.g: Probably “flash” — eyes blazing in anger or defiance.

chapters.n: The real problem, Eliphaz says, is that Job is turning his spirit against God and letting reckless words escape.

f.g: “Spirit” here can also mean anger or breath — Job is venting his rage at God.

chapters.n: Eliphaz repeats the main point of his night vision (4:17): no mortal can be truly clean or righteous before God.
If God cannot fully trust even his holy ones, and the heavens are not pure to him, mortals have no ground to claim innocence.

f.g: “Holy ones” — heavenly beings or angels, not human believers.

chapters.n: How much worse is a human being who gulps down sin as easily as drinking water. Eliphaz’s view of humanity is very dark.
Eliphaz announces a lesson from his own experience. Ironically, what follows assumes Job is the wicked man he describes.

f.g: Eliphaz relies on personal observation and tradition, not on revelation.

chapters.n: His teaching, he says, is ancient wisdom handed down from the fathers and openly passed on.
These ancestors received the land as theirs alone, with no foreigners to corrupt their teaching — so their tradition is pure.

f.g: No outsider — Eliphaz claims the wisdom is untainted by foreign ideas.

chapters.n: Eliphaz begins his portrait of the wicked: such a person lives in constant inner anguish, never knowing how many years he has left.

f.g: Writhes as in labor pains — continual torment.

chapters.n: Even in good times the wicked man hears frightening sounds. He expects disaster to strike at any moment.

f.g: A raider or plunderer; Job’s losses to raiders (1:15, 17) make this a pointed jab.

chapters.n: He has no hope of escaping his darkness and feels the sword waiting for him.

f.g: Marked out for violent death.

chapters.n: Eliphaz pictures him wandering in search of food, knowing that his day of ruin is close at hand.

f.g: A day of calamity and judgment.

chapters.n: Distress and anguish overwhelm him like a king charging into battle.

f.w: as a king ready to the battle
f.g: A powerful attacker prepared to strike.

chapters.n: The reason for his downfall: he has shaken his fist at God and tried to set himself up against the Almighty.

f.w: stretcheth out his hand against God
f.g: A gesture of defiance — perhaps meant to describe how Eliphaz sees Job’s protests.

chapters.n: The wicked man is pictured as a reckless warrior charging at God with head down behind a heavy shield.

f.g: The raised metal knobs on a shield (buckler = small shield).

chapters.n: His face and body are thick with fat — a picture of self-indulgent, arrogant prosperity that has made him callous.

f.g: Thick folds or rolls of fat.

chapters.n: In the end he lives among abandoned ruins, cities and homes soon to become heaps of rubble.

f.g: Destined to be piles of ruins.

chapters.n: His wealth will not last, and his possessions will not spread across the land.

f.g: Possibly “his holdings” or “his grain” — the meaning is uncertain.

chapters.n: He will never escape darkness. Like a tree scorched by fire, his branches wither, and God’s breath sweeps him away.

f.g: Probably God’s breath — a picture of divine judgment.

chapters.n: Eliphaz warns: whoever trusts in emptiness will be repaid with emptiness.

f.g: Emptiness, worthlessness — what has no substance.
Payment, reward.

chapters.n: His end will come before his time, and his branch will never be green again.
Like a vine dropping unripe grapes or an olive tree shedding blossoms, the wicked lose their fruit before it matures.

f.w: cast off his flower as the olive
f.g: Olive trees shed many blossoms; the image is of fruitfulness lost.

chapters.n: Communities of the godless will be left desolate, and fire will burn the homes of those who take bribes.

f.g: Hebrew ḥanef — the godless or profane.
Tents of those enriched by bribes — a hint at Job’s supposed corruption (compare 22:6-9).

chapters.n: Eliphaz ends with a birth image: the wicked conceive trouble and give birth to emptiness. He has described evil well but misjudged Job.
Job replies to Eliphaz’s second speech. Rather than defend himself point by point, he first tells his friends how their words feel to him.
Job has heard all this before. His friends came to comfort him (2:11), but their comfort only adds to his misery.

f.g: Literally “comforters of trouble” — people whose comfort brings more pain.

chapters.n: He turns Eliphaz’s charge of “windy words” (15:2) back on him: will your empty speeches ever end? What drives you to keep answering?

f.g: Literally “words of wind,” echoing Eliphaz’s jab in 15:2.

chapters.n: If their places were reversed, Job admits, he could easily pile up speeches and shake his head in scorn at them too.

f.g: A gesture of mockery or contempt.

chapters.n: But Job says he would use his words to strengthen and soothe them. He describes the kind of friend he wishes they were.

f.g: Assuage = ease or soften. Job models what real comfort looks like.

chapters.n: Neither speaking nor staying silent brings Job any relief. His pain stays with him either way.

f.g: Hold back, keep silent.

chapters.n: Job feels exhausted by God, who has stripped away his family and household. He shifts between speaking about God and to God.

f.g: Job’s household and family, now gone (1:13-19).

chapters.n: His shriveled, wasted body seems to testify against him — as if his suffering proves he is guilty, just as the friends claim.

f.g: Gauntness from illness; Job’s body has become a “witness” the friends use against him.

chapters.n: Job uses fierce animal imagery: he feels as if God has torn him like a beast and glared at him like an enemy.

f.w: gnasheth upon me with his teeth

chapters.n: Now a crowd joins in, gaping, slapping his face, and gathering against him. Many readers see in this a foreshadowing of the Savior’s mistreatment.
Job feels God has handed him over to wicked and ungodly people.

f.g: Job’s honest feeling — the reader knows from chapters 1–2 that Satan, not God’s hatred, is behind his trials.

chapters.n: Job was living in peace when God seemed to seize him by the neck, shake him apart, and set him up as a target.

f.w: set me up for his mark
f.g: Made me his target for arrows.

chapters.n: Surrounded by archers, Job feels pierced in his innermost being, his life spilled on the ground.

f.g: Kidneys — in Hebrew thought, the seat of the deepest emotions.
Bile; here a picture of his very life poured out.

chapters.n: Job is like a city wall battered breach after breach, with God charging at him like a mighty warrior.

f.g: Gap after gap broken in a wall during a siege.
A mighty warrior.

chapters.n: Job has sewn rough mourning cloth onto his skin and laid his dignity in the dust.

f.g: Coarse goat-hair cloth worn in mourning and repentance.
A symbol of strength and honor; to put it in the dust is to be utterly humbled.

chapters.n: His face is red and swollen with weeping, and deep darkness hangs over his eyes.

f.g: Deep darkness or gloom.

chapters.n: Yet Job insists none of this is because of violence or wrongdoing on his part, and his prayers are sincere.
Like Abel’s blood crying from the ground, Job pleads with the earth not to cover his blood — let his cry for justice never be silenced.
Here is a breakthrough of faith: even now Job believes he has a witness in heaven who knows the truth and will vouch for him.

f.g: One who testifies — an advocate who will speak for him.

chapters.n: His friends mock him, but Job weeps his tears toward God — he keeps turning to the very One he cannot understand.

f.g: Can also be read “my interpreters (or spokesmen) are my friends” — the Hebrew is ambiguous.

chapters.n: Job longs for someone who could plead his case with God the way a person argues for a friend. Christians hear here a longing for Christ, the Advocate with the Father.

f.w: plead for a man with God

chapters.n: Job expects to die soon and take the road from which no one returns, so he wants his name cleared before then.

f.w: the way whence I shall not return

chapters.n: Job continues: his spirit is broken, his life is snuffed out, and the grave is waiting for him.

f.g: Better “my spirit is broken.”
Extinguished, put out like a lamp.

chapters.n: He is surrounded by mockers, and he must keep watching their taunting.

f.g: Bitter taunting that provokes him.

chapters.n: Job asks God himself to put up a pledge for him, since no human friend will. He is asking God to guarantee his innocence.

f.g: A guarantee or bond posted for someone.
Shake hands on a deal — to become someone’s guarantor.

chapters.n: God has closed the friends’ minds to understanding, Job says, so he will not let them triumph.

f.g: Blinded their minds — they cannot see the truth of Job’s case.

chapters.n: Job quotes what sounds like a proverb: whoever betrays friends for gain will see his own children suffer. It warns the friends against their disloyalty.

f.g: Likely “denounces friends for a share of their property” — a betrayal of friendship.

chapters.n: God has made Job a proverb people use for misery. Once he was honored; now people spit in his face.

f.g: A saying or by-name for disgrace.
A small drum; but the Hebrew here likely means “one in whose face they spit.”

chapters.n: Grief has dimmed his eyes, and his body has wasted away to a mere shadow.

f.g: Limbs, parts of the body.

chapters.n: Job says upright people should be appalled at how he is treated and stirred against the godless.

f.g: Astonished, appalled.
The godless person.

chapters.n: A ringing statement of resolve: the righteous will keep to their path, and those with clean hands grow stronger and stronger. Job will not give up his integrity.
Job challenges his friends to come back and try again, because he has not found a single wise man among them.

f.w: I cannot find one wise man among you

chapters.n: His days are over and his plans are broken off — even the deepest desires of his heart.

f.g: Literally “possessions of my heart” — his cherished hopes.

chapters.n: His friends try to call his night day, offering cheerful promises of light when Job sees only darkness.

f.w: They change the night into day

chapters.n: All Job can look forward to is the grave as his home and darkness as his bed.

f.g: Hebrew sheol — the place of the dead.

chapters.n: Job speaks of decay as his family — calling corruption his father and the worm his mother and sister. He is at home only with death.

f.g: Decay, or “the pit.”

chapters.n: Where, then, is his hope? Who can see any hope left for him?
Job’s hope seems to go down with him into the gates of the grave. Even so, he will soon reach for a greater hope in chapter 19.

f.g: The gates of sheol, the realm of the dead.

f.w: rest together is in the dust

chapters.n: Bildad, the second friend, speaks again. His second speech is short, stinging, and entirely about the fate of the wicked.

f.g: Possibly a descendant of Shuah, a son of Abraham and Keturah.

chapters.n: Bildad tells Job to stop talking and think, so a real conversation can happen.

f.g: Pay attention, consider.

chapters.n: He is offended that Job treats the friends as dumb animals and considers them stupid.

f.g: Stupid or unclean.

chapters.n: Bildad says Job is tearing himself apart in anger. Does Job expect the whole world order to be rearranged just for him?

f.w: shall the rock be removed out of his place?
f.g: Will God change the fixed moral laws of the universe for your sake?

chapters.n: Bildad’s main point: the light of the wicked always goes out. Their life and success are snuffed like a fire.

f.w: light of the wicked shall be put out

chapters.n: The lamp in the wicked man’s tent grows dark — a picture of a household and family line coming to an end.

f.g: Lamp. A burning lamp in a home was a sign of life and continuing family.

chapters.n: His once-strong stride is cut short, and his own scheming brings him down.

f.g: Narrowed, hemmed in.

chapters.n: Bildad piles up hunting images: the wicked man walks into his own net and treads on a trap.

f.w: cast into a net by his own feet

chapters.n: A trap snaps on his heel and holds him tight.

f.g: A snare or trap (from “engine”).
Better “snare” or “noose” — another trap word.

chapters.n: A noose is hidden in the ground and a trap on his path. Bildad uses six words for traps in verses 8–10 to stress that escape is impossible.

f.g: A hidden noose or cord trap.

chapters.n: Terrors surround him and chase him at every step.
His strength is starved away, and disaster stands ready beside him.

f.g: Weakened by hunger, famished.

chapters.n: Disease eats away his skin and limbs. The “firstborn of death” is a vivid name for the deadliest disease — an unmistakable jab at Job’s own illness.

f.g: A poetic name for a deadly plague or disease.

chapters.n: He is torn from the security of his home and marched off to the “king of terrors” — death itself.

f.g: Death, personified as a ruler of the underworld.

chapters.n: Strangers will live in his tent, and burning sulfur will be scattered on his home, as at Sodom.

f.g: Burning sulfur, a sign of total judgment.

chapters.n: Like a tree, he withers from the roots up and his branches are cut off.

f.w: His roots shall be dried up

chapters.n: No one will remember him; his name will vanish from public life.
He will be driven from light into darkness and expelled from the world of the living.

f.g: Banished from the land of the living.

chapters.n: He will have no children or descendants left — a cruel jab, since Job’s children have died.

f.g: Nephew here means grandson or descendant.

chapters.n: People in the west and east alike will be horrified at his fate.

f.g: Possibly “those in the west … those in the east” — everyone everywhere.

chapters.n: Bildad’s conclusion: this is the fate of those who do not know God. He implies Job is one of them — but chapter 1 says otherwise.
Job answers Bildad. This chapter moves from the depths of despair to one of the greatest declarations of faith in all scripture.
Job asks how long his friends will keep tormenting him and crushing him with words.

f.g: Torment, grieve.

chapters.n: “Ten times” means “over and over.” Job says they are not ashamed to treat him so harshly.

f.g: An idiom for many times.
Wrong me, treat me harshly (the Hebrew is uncertain).

chapters.n: Even if Job has made some mistake, it is his own concern — it hasn’t harmed them, and they have no right to condemn him for it.

f.g: Made an unintentional mistake.

chapters.n: If the friends insist on lifting themselves above him and using his disgrace as evidence against him…

f.g: My humiliation — his suffering, which they treat as proof of guilt.

chapters.n: …then they should know that it is God who has thrown him down, not his own sin. Job answers Bildad’s trap imagery (18:8-10): the net is God’s.
Job cries “Violence!” but no one hears; he calls for help but finds no justice.

f.g: Literally “I cry, ‘Violence!’” — the call of someone being attacked.

chapters.n: God has walled off his road and covered his path in darkness — Job feels trapped with no way forward.
Job has been stripped of his honor and the crown of his reputation.

f.w: taken the crown from my head

chapters.n: He feels torn down on every side, his hope uprooted like a tree — a sad reversal of his earlier hope for a tree that sprouts again (14:7).
Job feels God’s anger burning against him, as though God counts him an enemy.
He pictures God’s troops building siege ramps and camping around his tent — overwhelming force against one small man.

f.g: Build up a siege ramp.

chapters.n: Now Job lists the people who have abandoned him, starting with his brothers and acquaintances.

f.w: put my brethren far from me

chapters.n: His relatives and closest friends have failed him and forgotten him.

f.g: Intimate friends, those who knew him well.

chapters.n: Even guests and servant girls in his house treat him like a foreigner.

f.g: Foreigner, outsider.

chapters.n: He calls his own servant and gets no answer, even when he begs.

f.g: Pleaded with him.

chapters.n: His wife finds his breath repulsive, and his own brothers are disgusted by him.

f.w: the children's sake of mine own body
f.g: Probably “my own brothers” (sons of my mother’s womb), since Job’s children have died.

chapters.n: Even little children make fun of him; when he gets up, they mock.
His closest friends now loathe him, and those he loved have turned against him.

f.g: Intimate friends, his inner circle.

chapters.n: He is skin and bones and has escaped death only by the narrowest margin — the origin of the phrase “by the skin of my teeth.”

f.g: A barely-there margin; the expression in English comes from this verse.

chapters.n: Job begs his friends for pity, since God’s hand has struck him. It is a raw, human plea for kindness.

f.w: the hand of God hath touched me

chapters.n: Why do they hound him as God seems to? Aren’t they satisfied with tearing at his flesh?

f.g: An idiom for slander — “eating someone’s flesh.”

chapters.n: Job longs for his words to be written down as a lasting record, so that future generations will know his testimony.

f.g: Inscribed on a scroll.

chapters.n: Better still, carved into rock with an iron chisel and filled with lead so they could never be erased.

f.g: An engraving tool and lead poured into carved letters to make them stand out.

chapters.n: The heart of the book: Job knows his Redeemer lives and will stand on the earth at the last day. Latter-day Saints see this as a testimony of Jesus Christ, the living Redeemer.

f.g: Hebrew go’el — a kinsman who rescues, avenges, or buys back a family member.

f.w: he shall stand at the latter day upon the earth

chapters.n: Even after his body decays, Job declares, in his flesh he will see God. Latter-day Saints read this as a clear witness of a literal, physical resurrection.

f.w: in my flesh shall I see God

chapters.n: Job will see God with his own eyes, personally, not through someone else — and his heart longs for that day.

f.g: Kidneys; the innermost self — “my heart faints with longing.”

chapters.n: Job warns the friends: if they keep saying the root of his trouble lies in him, they are wrong.

f.g: The cause of the trouble.
