chapters.n: He warns them to fear God’s judgment themselves, for their false accusations deserve it. In the end God does rebuke them (42:7).
Zophar, the third and bluntest friend, gives his second (and last) speech. He seems to ignore Job’s great statement of faith in chapter 19.

f.g: From Naamah, a place of uncertain location, perhaps in Arabia.

chapters.n: Zophar says his troubled thoughts push him to answer quickly.

f.g: Literally “because of my inner agitation” — he is upset and eager to reply.

chapters.n: He feels insulted by Job’s rebuke, and his understanding compels him to respond.

f.g: A rebuke that insults me — perhaps Job’s warning in 19:28-29.

chapters.n: Zophar appeals to what everyone has known since humans first lived on earth.

f.w: since man was placed upon earth
f.g: Literally “since Adam was placed on earth.”

chapters.n: His thesis: the triumph of the wicked is brief, and the joy of the godless lasts only a moment. There is truth here — Job’s mistake is in being labeled wicked.

f.w: the triumphing of the wicked is short

chapters.n: Even if the wicked man’s pride rises to the sky and his head touches the clouds…

f.w: his head reach unto the clouds

chapters.n: …he will perish like his own dung, and those who knew him will ask, “Where did he go?” Zophar’s language is deliberately crude.
He will vanish like a dream when you wake up, chased away like a vision of the night.
No eye that saw him will see him again; his home will know him no more.

f.w: neither shall his place any more behold him

chapters.n: His children will have to beg favor from the poor, and he will have to give back what he took by force.

f.g: Give back stolen property.

chapters.n: His body may be full of youthful vigor, but it will lie down with him in the dust.

f.g: Better “his youthful vigor” — the Hebrew word means youthfulness.

chapters.n: Zophar compares wickedness to a sweet treat that someone savors, rolling it under the tongue.
The wicked person loves sin so much he holds it in his mouth and won’t let it go.

f.g: Hold on to it, be reluctant to give it up.

chapters.n: But in his stomach the sweet food turns sour, becoming poison like snake venom.

f.g: Venom of cobras.

chapters.n: He gulps down riches but will vomit them up — God makes him disgorge them.
What he swallowed becomes snake poison that kills him. Sin carries its own deadly consequences.

f.g: Ancient people thought snakes struck with their tongues.

chapters.n: He will never enjoy the streams of honey and butter — images of plenty in a blessed land.

f.g: Butter = curds or cream; images of abundance.

chapters.n: He must give back what he gained and cannot enjoy the profits of his trading.

f.g: Repayment of what was taken.

chapters.n: Zophar names the crime: crushing and abandoning the poor and seizing houses he did not build.

f.w: oppressed and hath forsaken the poor

chapters.n: Because his greed is never satisfied, he will never know inner peace, and nothing he craves will be saved.

f.g: Contentment; his appetite is never satisfied.

chapters.n: Nothing escapes his appetite, so his prosperity will not last.

f.w: There shall none of his meat be left
f.g: He devours everything, leaving nothing behind.

chapters.n: At the height of his plenty, distress overtakes him, and every hand of misery strikes him.

f.g: In distress, in a tight place.

chapters.n: While he is filling his belly, God rains down his fury like a storm — an ironic “meal” of judgment.
He may run from an iron weapon, but a bronze-tipped arrow will pierce him.

f.g: Literally a bow of bronze.

chapters.n: The arrow is pulled out through his body, gleaming, and terrors come over him.

f.g: Liver or gallbladder — the arrow has pierced him through.

chapters.n: Total darkness waits for his treasures; a fire no human lit consumes him and whatever remains in his tent.

f.g: A fire not fanned by human breath — fire from God.

chapters.n: Heaven exposes his guilt and the earth rises as a witness against him. This seems to reply to Job’s hope for a heavenly witness (16:19).

f.w: The heaven shall reveal his iniquity

chapters.n: His household’s wealth will be carried off like a flood on the day of God’s anger.

f.g: Be swept away like rushing water.

chapters.n: Zophar sums up: this is God’s assigned portion for the wicked. His words are true of evil in general but cruelly misapplied to Job.

f.w: the heritage appointed unto him by God

chapters.n: Job replies to Zophar. In this speech he directly challenges the friends’ claim that the wicked always suffer quickly.
Job asks them simply to listen carefully. If they’ll just hear him out, that would be the best comfort they could give.

f.g: Your listening would be your comfort to me.

chapters.n: Let him speak — afterward they can go on mocking if they want.

f.g: Allow me, let me.

chapters.n: Job’s complaint is not against people but against God’s ways, so of course he is impatient and troubled.

f.g: He is wrestling with God, not merely with his friends.

chapters.n: Look at me, he says, and be shocked into silence.

f.w: lay your hand upon your mouth
f.g: A gesture of stunned silence.

chapters.n: Even thinking about what he is going to say makes him shudder.

f.w: trembling taketh hold on my flesh
f.g: Job is troubled by the hard truth he is about to state.

chapters.n: Job’s big question: why do the wicked live long, grow old, and become powerful? It contradicts Zophar’s whole speech.
Their children grow up and thrive around them — the very blessing Job lost.
Their homes are safe and peaceful; God’s rod of punishment doesn’t seem to touch them.

f.g: A symbol of God’s discipline or punishment.

chapters.n: Their herds breed successfully and never miscarry.

f.g: Breeds.
Does not miscarry.

chapters.n: Their children skip and play like lambs in a flock.

f.g: A picture of carefree, happy families.

chapters.n: They sing to tambourine and lyre and celebrate with flute music.

chapters.n: They spend their lives in prosperity and die quickly and peacefully, without long suffering.

f.w: in a moment go down to the grave
f.g: A quick, painless death — something Job, suffering slowly, would envy.

chapters.n: Yet these same people tell God to leave them alone; they don’t want to know his ways.

f.w: the counsel of the wicked is far from me

chapters.n: Turning Bildad’s words (18:5-6) into a question: how often does the lamp of the wicked actually go out? Not very often, Job suggests.

f.w: How oft is the candle of the wicked put out!

f.w: God layeth up his iniquity for his children

chapters.n: Let the wicked see their own ruin and drink God’s wrath personally.

One person dies at full strength, comfortable and secure…

f.g: Completely untroubled.

chapters.n: …well fed and healthy to the very bones.

f.g: Probably “his body is well nourished” (the Hebrew is uncertain).
Full of vigor and health.

chapters.n: Another dies bitter, never having enjoyed good things.

f.w: lie down alike in the dust

chapters.n: Job knows what the friends are thinking and the schemes they are plotting against him.

f.g: Plans, schemes.

chapters.n: They hint, “Where is the great man’s house now?” — meaning Job’s ruined estate proves his wickedness.

f.g: A thinly veiled reference to Job’s own fallen household.

chapters.n: Job tells them to ask travelers who have seen the world; they know the facts.

f.g: Signs, evidence, reports.

chapters.n: Travelers report that the wicked are often spared in the day of disaster. (Some translations read “spared,” others “reserved” for later judgment.)

f.w: reserved to the day of destruction
f.g: The Hebrew likely means the wicked are spared in calamity — or that their punishment is delayed until a future day.

chapters.n: Who dares to accuse a powerful wicked man to his face or repay him for what he has done?

f.w: declare his way to his face
f.g: Confront him openly about his conduct.

chapters.n: He is carried in honor to the grave, and a watch is kept over his tomb.

f.g: Literally “watch is kept over the tomb” — an honored burial.

f.g: The earth of the burial valley.

chapters.n: Job concludes: their comfort is empty, because their answers are false. Their neat theology doesn’t match reality.

f.g: Faithlessness or treachery — their answers betray the truth.

chapters.n: Eliphaz begins the third and final round of speeches. Now he openly accuses Job of specific sins — none of which are true.
Eliphaz asks whether a person’s goodness benefits God at all. A wise man helps himself, but God doesn’t need anything from us.

f.w: Is it any pleasure to the Almighty

chapters.n: Eliphaz asks whether God is punishing Job because Job is so pious. Obviously not, he implies — so it must be for sin.

f.g: Because of your reverence — because you are devout.

chapters.n: Now the open charge: “Isn’t your wickedness great and your sins endless?” Eliphaz has decided Job must be guilty.

f.g: Your sins without end — a charge the narrator has already refuted (1:1, 8).

chapters.n: He invents crimes: taking collateral from relatives without cause and stripping poor people of their clothes.

f.g: Taking a garment or item as security for a loan; the law limited this to protect the poor.

chapters.n: He accuses Job of refusing water to the tired and bread to the hungry — the opposite of the generosity Job describes in chapters 29 and 31.

f.g: Literally “the man of arm” — a powerful person who takes what he wants.

chapters.n: He claims Job sent widows away empty and crushed orphans. Job will answer this directly in 29:12-13 and 31:16-21.

f.g: Orphans — those most vulnerable in ancient society.

chapters.n: That, Eliphaz concludes, explains Job’s traps and sudden terrors.
Darkness blinds him and floods overwhelm him — images of total calamity.

f.g: Flood waters — a common image for overwhelming trouble.

chapters.n: Eliphaz points to God’s height above the stars to stress how great God is.

f.g: The vault or dome of the sky.

chapters.n: Eliphaz asks if Job will follow the ancient path of the wicked.

f.g: The well-worn path of past sinners.

f.w: the counsel of the wicked is far from me

chapters.n: The righteous rejoice and the innocent laugh when the wicked fall.

f.w: The righteous see it, and are glad

chapters.n: Accept God’s instruction and store his words in your heart.

f.w: lay up his words in thine heart

chapters.n: If Job returns to God and removes sin from his household, he will be restored.

chapters.n: God himself will be Job’s treasure and his precious silver.

f.g: Better “he would pay attention to me.”

f.g: Acquitted for good.

f.w: I shall come forth as gold

chapters.n: Job has followed close in God’s footsteps and kept his way without turning aside.

chapters.n: God will carry out what he has decreed for Job, and he has many such plans.

chapters.n: God has made Job’s heart faint; the Almighty has filled him with fear.

chapters.n: Job is not silenced by the darkness, though deep gloom covers his face. He keeps speaking despite it all.

f.w: I was not cut off before the darkness

f.g: Appointed times of judgment.

chapters.n: Job describes oppressors: they move boundary stones to steal land and seize flocks to graze as their own.

chapters.n: They take an orphan’s only donkey and seize a widow’s ox as collateral, leaving them helpless.

chapters.n: He mistreats the childless woman and does nothing good for the widow.

chapters.n: Yet God, by his power, prolongs the life of the mighty; they rise up even when they despair of living.

f.w: no man is sure of life
f.g: He rises even when he has given up hope of life.

chapters.n: God lets them feel secure, yet his eyes are on all their ways. Nothing escapes him.

f.w: his eyes are upon their ways

chapters.n: They are exalted for a short time, then brought low and cut off like heads of grain at harvest.

f.w: cut off as the tops of the ears of corn

chapters.n: God’s armies cannot be counted, and his light shines on everyone.

Job answers Bildad with biting irony before giving his own hymn to God’s power.
Sarcastically Job asks: what a help you have been to someone so weak! How you have rescued a powerless arm!

f.g: Job himself — Bildad’s words did nothing to help.

chapters.n: What wonderful advice you’ve given to someone without wisdom! What deep insight you have shared!

f.g: Shown abundant insight — said ironically.

chapters.n: Job asks who helped Bildad say these things — whose spirit was speaking through him? He implies the words were borrowed and empty.
Job now describes God’s power even over the realm of the dead. The departed spirits beneath the waters tremble before him.

f.g: Hebrew rephaim — the shades or spirits of the dead.

chapters.n: The place of the dead is laid bare before God; nothing is hidden from him, not even destruction itself.

f.g: Hebrew sheol — the world of departed spirits, not necessarily a place of punishment.
Hebrew Abaddon, a poetic name for the realm of the dead.

chapters.n: God stretches out the northern sky over empty space and hangs the earth on nothing — a striking image of God’s sustaining power.

f.g: Often symbolized God’s heavenly dwelling.

chapters.n: God wraps up water in clouds like skins of water, yet the clouds don’t burst under the weight.

f.w: bindeth up the waters in his thick clouds

f.g: Torn, split open.

The pillars holding up the sky shake and are stunned at God’s rebuke.

f.g: Poetic image of mountains that seem to hold up the sky.

chapters.n: By his power God calms (or stirs) the sea, and by his skill he strikes down Rahab, the proud sea monster.

f.g: Hebrew Rahab — a poetic name for a chaos monster of the sea, symbolizing forces opposed to God.

chapters.n: By his breath the skies became clear, and his hand pierced the fleeing serpent. God has defeated every power of chaos.

The “gliding serpent,” a symbol of chaos and evil.

chapters.n: All these wonders are just the edges of God’s ways — a mere whisper. Who could ever understand the full thunder of his power?

f.w: how little a portion is heard of him?

chapters.n: Job continues his discourse. With no further reply from Zophar, Job now delivers his closing statements (chapters 27–31).

f.g: Hebrew mashal — a formal discourse or poem, not just a short story.

chapters.n: Job swears an oath by the living God — the same God he feels has denied him justice and made his life bitter.

chapters.n: As long as he has breath — the breath God himself gave — Job makes his promise.

chapters.n: He holds tightly to his righteousness, and his conscience does not condemn him for any day of his life.

chapters.n: What hope does a godless person have when God takes his life, no matter how much he gained?

chapters.n: Will God hear his cry when trouble comes? By contrast, Job still cries to God.

Job promises to teach his friends about God’s ways and hold nothing back.

f.g: Concerning God’s power and actions.

chapters.n: They have all seen these things themselves — so why speak such nonsense?

f.g: Empty, foolish — literally “breath.”

chapters.n: Many children may be born to him, but they fall by the sword or go hungry.

f.w: multiplied, it is for the sword

chapters.n: People clap their hands in scorn and hiss him from his place — signs of contempt and relief at his fall.

No one has prescribed God’s ways for him, and no one can rightly say he did wrong.

f.g: Appointed, commanded.

chapters.n: Remember to praise God’s work, which people have sung about.
Everyone has seen it, even if only from far away.

f.g: Mortals see God’s works only partially, from a distance.

chapters.n: God is so great that we cannot fully understand him; his years cannot be counted.
Elihu begins describing the rain cycle: God draws up droplets of water, and they become rain from the mist.

f.w: maketh small the drops of water
f.g: Draws up drops of water — evaporation.

chapters.n: The clouds pour it down in showers on people.

f.g: Fall in drops.

chapters.n: Who can understand how clouds spread out, or the thunder that roars from God’s pavilion?

f.g: His canopy or pavilion — the storm clouds.

chapters.n: He spreads lightning around himself and covers the depths of the sea.

f.g: Lightning.

chapters.n: Through storms God governs the nations — bringing both judgment and abundant food.
He fills his hands with lightning and commands it to strike its target.

f.w: With clouds he covereth the light
f.g: Better “he covers his hands with lightning.”

chapters.n: The thunder announces his coming; even the cattle sense the storm approaching. The scene is being set for the whirlwind of chapter 38.

f.w: the cattle also concerning the vapour
f.g: Even livestock sense the coming storm.

chapters.n: As a storm seems to roll in, Elihu’s heart pounds and leaps at the sound.

f.g: Elihu may be describing a real storm approaching — the storm from which God will speak.

chapters.n: Listen to the thunder of God’s voice and the rumbling from his mouth!

f.g: Thunder, pictured as God’s voice.

chapters.n: He sends it across the whole sky, and his lightning to the ends of the earth.

f.w: his lightning unto the ends of the earth

chapters.n: After the flash comes the roar; God thunders with majestic voice and doesn’t hold back the lightning.

f.g: His majestic voice.

chapters.n: God thunders wonderfully; he does great things beyond our understanding.

f.w: great things doeth he, which we cannot comprehend

chapters.n: He tells the snow, “Fall on the earth,” and commands both light showers and heavy downpours.
In winter storms God brings all human work to a stop so that people will recognize his work.

f.w: He sealeth up the hand of every man
f.g: He halts human labor through bad weather.

chapters.n: Animals take shelter in their dens.
The storm comes from its chamber in the south, and cold from the scattering north winds.

f.g: Storm, tempest.

chapters.n: By God’s breath ice forms and broad waters freeze solid.

f.g: Narrowed, frozen fast.

f.w: By the breath of God frost is given

chapters.n: He loads the clouds with moisture and scatters his lightning through them.

f.g: Loads, burdens.
Lightning-cloud.

chapters.n: The clouds swirl at his direction, carrying out everything he commands across the world.

f.g: By his guidance, steering.

chapters.n: God sends storms for different purposes — to correct, to water his land, or to show mercy.

f.w: whether for correction, or for his land, or for mercy

chapters.n: Elihu calls on Job to stop and consider God’s wonders — just what God is about to ask Job to do.

f.w: stand still, and consider the wondrous works of God

chapters.n: Does Job know how God orders the clouds or makes lightning flash?

f.g: Set them in order.

chapters.n: Does he understand how clouds float in balance — the wonders of the One perfect in knowledge?

f.g: How clouds hang suspended in the air.

chapters.n: Job swelters in his clothes when the hot south wind stills the land.

f.g: The hot desert wind from the south.

chapters.n: Can Job, like God, spread out the sky, hard as a mirror of cast bronze?

f.g: A mirror of polished cast metal — ancient mirrors were bronze.

chapters.n: Tell us what to say to God — we can’t prepare a case because we are in the dark.

f.g: Because of our ignorance.

chapters.n: Should anyone tell God, “I want to speak”? Wouldn’t that be asking to be swallowed up? Elihu warns Job about demanding a hearing.

f.w: surely he shall be swallowed up
f.g: He would be overwhelmed.

chapters.n: No one can look at the sun when it shines in the skies after the wind has swept the clouds away.

f.w: the bright light which is in the clouds
f.g: The sun, dazzling in a cleared sky.

chapters.n: Out of the north comes golden splendor; God is clothed in awesome majesty. Elihu’s speech ends just as God appears.

f.g: Literally “gold” — golden radiance, perhaps the glow of God’s glory.
Awe-inspiring majesty.

chapters.n: We cannot reach the Almighty; he is great in power and justice and will not violate righteousness.

f.g: He does not oppress or pervert justice.

chapters.n: That is why people revere him; he does not regard those who think themselves wise. The stage is set for the Lord to speak.

f.w: he respecteth not any that are wise of heart

chapters.n: At last the Lord answers Job — not with an explanation of his suffering, but with his presence. That God speaks at all is itself an answer to Job’s plea. Latter-day Saints understand the LORD (Jehovah) as the premortal Jesus Christ.

f.g: Small capitals render God’s covenant name YHWH (Jehovah), used here for the first time since chapters 1–2.
A storm or tempest — a common setting for God’s appearances.

chapters.n: God asks who is clouding his plan with words that lack understanding. Job has spoken honestly, but without the full picture.

f.g: Obscures God’s purpose or design.

chapters.n: God tells Job to brace himself like a man, for now God will ask the questions. Job wanted a hearing — now he has one, but on God’s terms.

f.g: Tuck up your robe into your belt — get ready for action or contest.

chapters.n: The first question: where was Job when God laid the earth’s foundations? Latter-day Saints recall that we did exist then, as spirits, though we do not remember it.

f.w: Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth?

chapters.n: Who determined its measurements and stretched a measuring line across it? God is pictured as a master builder.

f.g: A builder’s measuring cord.

chapters.n: What are its foundations set on, and who laid its cornerstone? The cornerstone is a familiar symbol of Christ.

When the earth was founded, the morning stars sang and all the sons of God shouted for joy. Latter-day Saints see here the premortal council, where God’s spirit children rejoiced at the plan of salvation.

f.w: all the sons of God shouted for joy

chapters.n: Who shut the sea behind doors when it burst out like a baby from the womb? The fearsome sea is pictured as God’s infant.

f.w: shut up the sea with doors

chapters.n: God wrapped the newborn sea in clouds as clothing and in darkness as a baby’s swaddling cloth.

f.g: A strip of cloth wrapped around a newborn.

chapters.n: He fixed its limits with bars and doors.

f.g: The boundary God decreed for the sea.

chapters.n: He told the sea, “This far and no farther; here your proud waves must stop.” God sets limits even on chaos.

f.w: Hitherto shalt thou come, but no further

chapters.n: Has Job ever commanded the morning to come or shown the dawn its place?

f.g: Dawn, daybreak.

chapters.n: Dawn grabs the edges of the earth like a blanket and shakes the wicked out of it — for evildoers love darkness.

f.w: that the wicked might be shaken out of it

chapters.n: In morning light the earth takes shape like clay under a seal, and its features stand out like folds in a garment.

f.g: A signet ring pressed into soft clay leaves a clear image — so dawn reveals the landscape.

chapters.n: The wicked lose their “light” — the darkness they work in — and their raised arm is broken.

f.g: An arm raised in violence or defiance.

chapters.n: Has Job traveled to the springs of the sea or walked on the floor of the deep?

f.g: The hidden sources of the ocean.

chapters.n: Has he seen the gates of death or the doors of deep darkness? God alone has authority over death. Christ himself would later open those gates.
Does Job understand how vast the earth is? Let him say so if he knows it all.
Where does light live? Where is darkness’s home?
Could Job lead them back to their homes or find the paths there?

f.g: Its territory or boundary.

chapters.n: God teases gently: surely Job knows, since he was born back then and has lived so many years! The irony humbles without crushing.
Has Job entered the storehouses where snow and hail are kept?

f.g: Storehouses — ancient poetry pictured weather kept in heavenly warehouses.

chapters.n: God holds these in reserve for times of trouble and battle.

f.w: the day of battle and war

chapters.n: What is the path to where lightning is scattered or where the east wind spreads over the earth?

f.g: Possibly lightning distributed across the sky.

chapters.n: Who carved channels for downpours and a path for the thunderstorm?

f.w: a way for the lightning of thunder

chapters.n: God sends rain even on land where no human lives. Creation isn’t only about us — God cares for places no one sees.

f.w: on the wilderness, wherein there is no man

chapters.n: He waters desolate wasteland and makes tender grass sprout.

f.w: the bud of the tender herb

chapters.n: Does the rain have a father? Who fathered the dewdrops? Only God is their source.
From whose womb did ice come, and who gave birth to the frost from the sky?

f.g: White frost.
Given birth to, produced.

chapters.n: Water hardens like stone, and the surface of the deep freezes.

f.g: Frozen hard as stone.

chapters.n: Can Job tie together the cluster of the Pleiades or loosen Orion’s belt? God moves the constellations; humans can only watch.

f.g: The “Seven Sisters,” a star cluster.
The constellation of the hunter.

chapters.n: Can he lead out the constellations in their seasons or guide the Bear with her cubs?

f.g: Probably the constellations of the zodiac or a particular star group.
Probably the Great Bear (Big Dipper) with its stars as “sons.”

chapters.n: Does Job know the laws that govern the heavens or set their rule over the earth?
Can he shout to the clouds and have them drench him with rain?

f.w: lift up thy voice to the clouds

chapters.n: Can he send lightning bolts on their way and have them report, “Here we are”?

f.g: Lightning pictured as obedient servants reporting for duty.

chapters.n: Who put wisdom in the heart or understanding in the mind? (Some translate these as birds — the ibis and rooster — said to sense weather.)

f.g: Possibly “the ibis,” a bird thought to predict the Nile’s flooding.
Possibly “the rooster,” which announces dawn.

chapters.n: Who is wise enough to count the clouds, or can tip over the water jars of heaven…

f.g: Water-skins of the sky — rain clouds.

chapters.n: …when dust becomes hard and clods of earth stick together in drought?

f.g: Dry earth clumps hard before the rain.

chapters.n: God turns to animals. Can Job hunt prey for the lioness or satisfy hungry young lions?

f.w: Wilt thou hunt the prey for the lion?

chapters.n: …when they crouch in their dens or lie in wait in the thicket?

f.g: Crouch, lie down.
Hiding place, thicket.

chapters.n: Who provides food for the raven when its chicks cry to God, wandering in hunger? God cares for even the least-regarded birds — and surely for Job.

f.w: Who provideth for the raven his food?

chapters.n: The Lord continues with a tour of wild animals. Does Job know when mountain goats give birth or watch over deer as they calve?

f.g: The ibex, a mountain goat of the Near East.
Female deer.

chapters.n: Can he count the months of their pregnancy or know their time to give birth?

f.g: The term of their pregnancy.

chapters.n: They crouch, give birth, and are freed from labor pains — all without human help. God attends to births no human sees.

f.g: Deliver their young, ending their labor pains.

chapters.n: Their young grow strong in the open field, then leave and don’t come back.

f.g: Healthy, strong.
Here the open field or grain.

chapters.n: Who set the wild donkey free and untied its ropes?

f.g: The onager, a wild donkey that can’t be tamed.

chapters.n: God gave it the wilderness for a home and salt flats for its dwelling.

f.g: Salt land, salt flats.

chapters.n: It laughs at the noise of the city and never hears a driver’s shouts. It is free in a way no domesticated animal is.

f.g: A taskmaster who drives working animals.

chapters.n: It roams the mountains for pasture, searching for anything green.

f.g: Forages freely across the hills.

chapters.n: Will the wild ox agree to serve Job or spend the night by his feeding trough?

f.g: Hebrew re’em — the wild ox (aurochs), a huge and powerful animal, not a mythical horse.
Manger, feeding trough.

chapters.n: Can Job tie it with a rope to plow a furrow, or make it harrow the valleys behind him?

f.g: Break up plowed ground.

chapters.n: Will he trust it because it’s strong, and leave his heavy work to it?

f.w: wilt thou leave thy labour to him?
f.g: Will you rely on it to do your farm work?

chapters.n: Can he count on it to bring in his grain and gather it to his threshing floor?

f.g: Threshing floor.

chapters.n: The ostrich flaps its wings proudly, but they aren’t like the stork’s feathers — it can’t fly.

f.g: Better “ostriches.”
Possibly “the stork,” a bird known for caring for its young.

chapters.n: She leaves her eggs on the ground and lets them warm in the sand.

f.g: Ostriches lay eggs in shallow pits in the sand.

chapters.n: She forgets that a foot could crush them or a wild animal trample them.

f.w: the wild beast may break them
f.g: Her nests are easily disturbed.

chapters.n: She treats her young harshly, as if they weren’t hers, and doesn’t worry that her labor might be wasted.
God didn’t give her wisdom or a share of understanding. God made creatures with odd, even comical traits — and delights in them anyway.

f.w: God hath deprived her of wisdom
f.g: An affectionate, humorous description of the ostrich’s apparent carelessness.

chapters.n: Yet when she spreads her wings to run, she laughs at horse and rider — she can outrun them.

f.w: she scorneth the horse and his rider
f.g: Ostriches can run very fast, about 40 miles per hour.

chapters.n: Did Job give the war horse its strength or clothe its neck with a flowing mane?

f.g: Probably “with a mane” — the Hebrew word suggests quivering or rippling.

chapters.n: Can Job make it leap like a locust? Its proud snorting is terrifying.

f.g: As a locust — leaping and bounding.
Awe-inspiring, frightening.

chapters.n: It paws the valley floor, delights in its strength, and charges into the battle line.

f.w: goeth on to meet the armed men
f.g: Charges straight at the enemy.

chapters.n: It laughs at fear, is never frightened, and doesn’t turn back from the sword.

f.g: Laughs at danger.

chapters.n: Arrows rattle in the quiver against its side, along with flashing spear and javelin.

f.g: A case for arrows.

chapters.n: Trembling with excitement, it devours the ground and can’t stand still when the trumpet sounds.

f.g: Gallops furiously.

chapters.n: At the trumpet blast it snorts “Aha!” and smells the battle from far off, with commanders shouting.

f.g: An exclamation of eagerness — “Aha!”

chapters.n: Does the hawk soar by Job’s wisdom and spread its wings toward the south in migration?

f.w: stretch her wings toward the south
f.g: Migrate — many birds of prey pass through the Near East each year.

chapters.n: Does the eagle rise at Job’s command and build its nest high up?

f.g: Possibly the griffon vulture, which nests on high cliffs.

chapters.n: It lives on cliffs, resting on rocky crags and strongholds.

f.g: An inaccessible fortress-like crag.

chapters.n: From there it scans for food; its eyes spot prey from far away.

f.g: Birds of prey have remarkably keen vision.

chapters.n: Its young feed on blood, and wherever the dead lie, it is there. Even harsh parts of nature are under God’s care and design.

f.w: where the slain are, there is she

chapters.n: After his first speech, the Lord pauses and invites Job to respond.
Will the one who argues with the Almighty correct him? Whoever accuses God should answer now.

f.g: Argues, brings a lawsuit against.
One who criticizes or accuses God.

chapters.n: Job answers the Lord directly for the first time.
Job admits he is small and unworthy; he puts his hand over his mouth. The man who once silenced princes (29:9) is now silent before God.

f.g: I am insignificant, of little account — not “wicked.”

f.w: I will lay mine hand upon my mouth

chapters.n: He has spoken once, even twice, but he won’t say any more. Job yields, though full repentance comes in 42:1-6.

f.g: A Hebrew idiom (“once… twice”) meaning “I have said enough.”

chapters.n: The Lord speaks again from the storm, beginning his second speech.
Again God tells Job to brace himself and answer his questions.

f.w: Gird up thy loins now like a man

chapters.n: God names the real issue: will Job discredit God’s justice — condemn God — just to prove himself right? Job can be innocent without God being unjust.

f.g: Annul, overturn my justice.

f.w: wilt thou condemn me, that thou mayest be righteous?

chapters.n: Does Job have an arm like God’s, or can he thunder with a voice like his?

f.g: The arm symbolizes power.

chapters.n: Let Job dress himself in majesty, dignity, glory, and splendor — the royal robes of God.
Let him unleash his fury and humble every proud person he sees.

f.g: Bring him down, humble him.

chapters.n: Let him bring down the proud and crush the wicked where they stand.
Let him bury them all in the dust and shroud their faces in the grave.

f.g: Wrap them in the hidden place — the grave.

chapters.n: Then God would admit Job’s own power could save him. The point: only God can rule the world in justice; Job cannot save himself.

f.w: thine own right hand can save thee

chapters.n: God describes Behemoth, a huge beast he made just as he made Job. Many think it is the hippopotamus, described in poetic grandeur as a symbol of untamable strength.

f.g: A Hebrew plural of majesty meaning “the beast of beasts” — possibly the hippopotamus.
Job and Behemoth are both God’s creatures.

chapters.n: Its power is in its hips and the muscles of its belly.

f.g: Hips, lower body.

chapters.n: Its tail stiffens like a cedar, and the sinews of its thighs are knit together.

f.w: He moveth his tail like a cedar
f.g: Stiffens or sways its tail like a tree trunk.
Thighs (or reproductive organs).

chapters.n: Its bones are like bronze tubes and its limbs like iron bars.

f.g: Bronze.

chapters.n: It is first among God’s works; only its Maker can approach it with a sword.

f.w: the chief of the ways of God
f.g: Literally “the first of God’s ways” — echoing wisdom in Proverbs 8:22.

chapters.n: The hills provide its food, where wild animals play peacefully around it.

f.w: where all the beasts of the field play

chapters.n: It lies under lotus plants, hidden in reeds and marshes.

f.g: Lotus plants.
Marshes, swamps.

chapters.n: The lotus shades it, and the willows by the stream surround it.

f.g: Poplars or willows along a riverbank.

chapters.n: Even if the river rages, it isn’t alarmed; it stays calm though a flood like the Jordan surges against its mouth.

f.g: Better “if the river rages, he is not alarmed.”
Used here as a symbol of a mighty, rushing river.

chapters.n: Can anyone capture it while it watches, or pierce its nose with a hook? No human can master it — but God can.

f.g: Better “can anyone pierce his nose with a snare?”

chapters.n: God now describes Leviathan, a terrifying sea creature. It may be a crocodile pictured larger than life, and it also symbolizes the forces of chaos that only God can master. Can Job catch it with a fishhook?

f.g: A great sea monster — possibly the crocodile, and in poetry a symbol of chaos and evil.

chapters.n: Can Job put a rope through its nose or pierce its jaw with a hook, as people did with captured fish or prisoners?

f.w: bore his jaw through with a thorn
f.g: Fish were sometimes kept on a hook or ring through the jaw.

chapters.n: Will Leviathan beg Job for mercy or speak to him gently?

f.g: Pleas for mercy.

chapters.n: Will it make a covenant to be Job’s servant forever?
Can Job play with it like a pet bird or put it on a leash for his young daughters?

f.g: Leash him as a pet for girls.

chapters.n: Will traders bargain over it or divide it among merchants like a catch of fish?

f.g: Partners, trading guilds.
Literally “Canaanites,” who were known as traders.

chapters.n: Can Job fill its hide with harpoons or its head with fishing spears?

f.g: Harpoons.

chapters.n: Just lay a hand on it once — you will remember the fight and never try again!

f.w: remember the battle, do no more
f.g: You’ll never forget the struggle.

chapters.n: Any hope of capturing it is false; just seeing it knocks a person flat.

f.w: cast down even at the sight of him
f.g: Overwhelmed by fear just by looking.

chapters.n: No one is fierce enough to provoke it. Then who could stand against God, who made it? This is the heart of the speech.

f.w: who then is able to stand before me?

chapters.n: Who has given God anything first, so that God owes him? Everything under heaven belongs to God.

f.w: whatsoever is under the whole heaven is mine

f.g: Gone before, given first (old meaning).

chapters.n: God will not keep silent about Leviathan’s limbs, its great strength, and its graceful form.

f.g: Graceful build.

chapters.n: Who can strip off its outer armor or approach it with a double bridle?

f.g: Its outer coat — its scaly hide.

chapters.n: Who would dare open its jaws, ringed with terrifying teeth?

f.g: Its jaws.

chapters.n: Its back has rows of shields, sealed tightly together. (A crocodile’s back is covered with bony plates.)

f.g: Possibly “his back is rows of shields.”

chapters.n: The scales lie so close that no air can get between them.

f.w: no air can come between them
f.g: Impenetrable armor.

chapters.n: They are welded together and cannot be pried apart.

f.g: Separated, split apart.

chapters.n: Its sneezes flash with light, and its eyes glow like the rays of dawn.

f.g: Sneezes, snortings.
The first beams of dawn.

chapters.n: Flames shoot from its mouth and sparks fly out — poetic language that makes Leviathan a dragon-like symbol of overwhelming power.

f.g: Torches, firebrands.

chapters.n: Smoke pours from its nostrils like steam from a boiling pot over burning reeds.

f.g: A boiling pot.

chapters.n: Its breath sets coals on fire, and a flame comes from its mouth.
Strength lives in its neck, and terror dances ahead of it.

f.w: sorrow is turned into joy before him
f.g: Better “dismay leaps before him.”

chapters.n: The folds of its flesh are tightly joined and immovable.

f.g: Folds, layers.

chapters.n: Its heart is as hard as rock, hard as a lower millstone.

f.g: The lower millstone, which was especially hard to withstand constant grinding.

chapters.n: When it rises, even the mighty are terrified and lose control in panic.

f.w: by reason of breakings they purify themselves
f.g: Better “they are beside themselves with fear.”

chapters.n: Sword, spear, dart, or javelin — none can harm it.

f.g: Here probably a javelin (elsewhere, a coat of mail).

chapters.n: It treats iron like straw and bronze like rotten wood.

f.g: Bronze.

chapters.n: Arrows don’t make it run, and slingstones are like chaff to it.

f.g: Stones hurled from a sling.

chapters.n: Clubs are like straw, and it laughs at the rattle of a javelin.

f.w: he laugheth at the shaking of a spear

chapters.n: Its underside is like jagged pottery, leaving marks in the mud like a threshing sledge.

f.g: Sharp potsherds.
A threshing sledge — a board studded with stones.

chapters.n: It makes the deep churn like a boiling pot and the sea like a pot of mixing perfume.

f.g: A jar of perfume being stirred.

chapters.n: It leaves a glittering wake behind it; one would think the deep had white hair.

f.g: White-haired, gray — the foaming wake.

chapters.n: Nothing on earth equals it — a creature made without fear.

f.w: Upon earth there is not his like

chapters.n: It looks down on all the proud; it is king over every proud beast. Only God is above it — and Job is invited to trust the God who rules even this.

f.w: a king over all the children of pride

chapters.n: Job gives his final reply to the Lord — humble, honest, and transformed.
Job confesses that God can do anything and that no purpose of his can be stopped.

f.w: no thought can be withholden from thee
f.g: No plan of yours can be thwarted.

chapters.n: Quoting God’s question (38:2), Job admits he spoke of things he didn’t understand — wonders beyond his knowledge.

f.w: Who is he that hideth counsel without knowledge?

chapters.n: He quotes God again (38:3; 40:7): “Listen, and I will question you.” Job now takes the role of the learner.

f.w: I will demand of thee, and declare thou unto me

chapters.n: The turning point of the book: Job had known about God by hearsay, but now he has seen God for himself. Personal revelation has replaced secondhand religion.
So Job retracts his complaints and repents in dust and ashes. He isn’t confessing hidden sins — he is humbly yielding his demand that God explain himself.

f.g: Or “I retract my words” — the Hebrew can mean reject or recant.

chapters.n: The prose story resumes. The Lord tells Eliphaz he is angry with him and his two friends, because they didn’t speak rightly about God as Job did. Honest wrestling pleased God more than pious falsehood.

f.w: ye have not spoken of me the thing that is right

chapters.n: The friends must offer seven bulls and seven rams and ask Job to pray for them. God will accept Job’s prayer and spare them. Job, once condemned by them, becomes their intercessor — a type of Christ.

f.w: my servant Job shall pray for you

f.g: An offering entirely burned on the altar, symbolizing complete dedication and atonement.

chapters.n: The three friends obey, and the Lord accepts Job’s prayer.

f.g: Literally “lifted up Job’s face” — showed him favor.

chapters.n: The Lord restores Job’s fortunes after he prays for his friends — and gives him twice as much as before. Forgiving those who hurt him comes before the blessing.

f.g: Restored his fortunes.

chapters.n: His family and old friends finally come, eat with him, and comfort him, each giving a piece of silver and a gold ring.

f.g: Hebrew qesitah, an ancient unit of value, also mentioned in Genesis 33:19.

chapters.n: The Lord blesses Job’s later life more than his early life. His herds are exactly double those in 1:3.

He has seven sons and three daughters again — the same number as before. Many note that his children are not “doubled” because his first children were not lost forever; Latter-day Saints believe families can continue beyond death.
Unusually, the daughters are named: Jemimah (“dove”), Keziah (“cassia,” a fragrant spice), and Keren-happuch (“horn of eye-paint”).

f.g: Dove.
Cassia — a cinnamon-like spice.
Horn (container) of eye cosmetic — a symbol of beauty.

chapters.n: Job’s daughters were the most beautiful in the land, and remarkably he gave them an inheritance alongside their brothers — a rare act of generosity and honor for women in that era.

f.w: gave them inheritance among their brethren

chapters.n: Job lives 140 more years and sees four generations of descendants.
Job dies old and full of days — a satisfying, complete life. His story teaches that faith can survive suffering without having every question answered.
